Some were directly employed by Microsoft, others worked for subcontractors in countries potentially hostile to the UK, from Israel to Egypt, China and Kazakhstan. “You’ve seen the list of their sub-processors of people who have access to customer data,” said Michels. “It’s a long list.”
Some of the engineers could access data, such as UK police data, directly as part of customer support. Many more could see key features of what the data included.
![Exterior of a Microsoft datacentre in the Netherlands.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/2e6cebbdc93edfcd04f7445de550e1e428c6cb16/0_0_5643_3913/master/5643.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Microsoft said it had “strong guardrails” around data access by engineers.
Douwe Korff, a professor of international law at London Metropolitan University, said the police statement that “we do not expect any sharing [of our data] with the US government” was “typical lawyers’ wriggling”.
“The risk is obvious, even though the providers of the cloud and the government both have an interest in talking it down,” he said.
Michels said: “As a cloud customer, if you’re relying on a contractual commitment from a cloud provider not to hand over data when forced to under foreign law, that is not worth much more than the piece of paper it’s written on.”
US law, including the Cloud Act, allows US authorities to access any data held by US cloud companies, including data held abroad. US authorities do not need a warrant to do this, and they can require US companies to not disclose such access to cloud customers.
Microsoft, Amazon and Google have insisted they would fight such requests, said Korff. But there is “nothing that is legally binding” that would prevent them from sharing other governments’ data if US authorities demanded it.
In response to a query from the Guardian, Microsoft said it “has never provided UK government data in response to any US or global authority request”. It added in a follow-up that it was bound by its “contractual commitments”.
“If UK law prohibits us from turning over data to another government, that is a binding law that would govern our response to any hypothetical demand,” it said.
‘The security guys expected a big breach by now’
The Guardian spoke to six people who have closely followed the country’s data storage arrangements over the past decade. Several of them said that senior leaders did not view dependence on US tech companies as a concern, and trusted them not to give data to US authorities.
“Government security departments are painfully aware of all the risks,” said Mark Butcher, a cloud expert who acts as a strategic adviser across government. “But the way that most senior leaders talk about it is: ‘Well, we’ve been reassured by Microsoft that it would never happen.’”
But the source who has held senior policing roles said: “All the security guys I worked with when this policy came in expected a big breach by now, and we know it will take that to change the police’s position.
“The truth is, however, the level of logging and information in the cloud systems would not necessarily tell us if there was a problem. We really don’t know if the data has been breached or not.”
summary: Vast amounts of sensitive UK police data, including criminal records and victim statements stored on Microsoft Azure, were deemed vulnerable to compromise by foreign actors and the US government in an official security assessment. Despite these identified risks from a 2017 police meeting and ongoing warnings from specialists regarding US laws and global access by engineers, nearly all UK police forces migrated their data to the platform. While police and Microsoft maintain that strict controls and contracts protect the data, experts argue that these safeguards are inadequate against potential foreign access.
key_points: Over 40 UK police forces store sensitive data, including criminal records and victim statements, on Microsoft's Azure cloud platform.
A 2017 UK security assessment warned that the platform was vulnerable to cybercriminals and potential 'US government insider attackers'.
US laws, such as the Cloud Act, allow US authorities to compel US tech companies to hand over data stored abroad without a warrant.
Experts and Microsoft engineers state that Microsoft's global network and numerous support personnel mean data can be accessed internationally, making data sovereignty guarantees unreliable.

title: iPhone 18 Pro: Using the New Variable Aperture Lens
author: Tim Hardwick
content:
Like the iPhone 17 Pro models, the new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have three rear cameras – a 48MP Fusion Main lens, an 8x48MP Telephoto lens, and a 48MP Ultra Wide lens. They also share the same focal lengths and resolutions as their predecessors. The big upgrade this year though is the new variable aperture on the Main camera. Let's dive in.
![Apple iPhone 18 Pro 2up 16x9 1](https://images.macrumors.com/t/IGFWDLa9PJ79ihtmZ0OuIdbI3ew=/400x0/article-new/2026/09/Apple-iPhone-18-Pro-2up-16x9-1.jpg?lossy)
Aperture is what controls how much light enters the lens and hits the sensor. If too little light hits that sensor, images tend to be blurry and/or grainy. To compensate, the shutter has to stay open longer, or it has to turn on Night Mode. The problem with this approach is that the longer the shutter stays open or Night Mode is engaged, the more likely that the imagery will be blurry. Even still photos can lack sharpness and definition.
The solution is to use a variable aperture lens that is physically able to let more or less light in depending on the shot, which in turn allows for variations in shutter speed. The iPhone 18 Pro models can do this automatically, or you can take over the process manually for more stylistic control.
To achieve this, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max trade a fixed ƒ/1.78 aperture for a four-stop variable aperture ranging from ƒ/1.48 to ƒ/4.0, delivering around 50 percent better low-light performance and giving photographers optical control over depth of field that the iPhone has never offered before.
![variable aperture iphone 18 pro](https://images.macrumors.com/t/e1DduxQhHkNYPzqPAuIqq9-IZPY=/400x0/article-new/2026/09/variable-aperture-iphone-18-pro.jpg?lossy)
As mentioned, you can leave the iPhone 18 Pro to do its thing with the new variable aperture, or you can take control of it manually. Here's how it's done:
- In the Camera app, tap the button with six dots at the bottom-right of the interface.
- Select Lens Aperture from the control pane.
- Tap one of the four circles to set the aperture: from left to right they range ƒ/1.48, ƒ1.8, ƒ2.8, and finally, ƒ/4.0.
- If you change your mind, tap the Auto button on the left to let the iPhone automatically control the aperture.
![variable aperture](https://images.macrumors.com/t/DKTg5TTctG3KxradJOTvUaCAabA=/400x0/article-new/2026/09/iphone-18-pro-lens-aperture.jpeg?lossy)
Try experimenting with different aperture settings to see how they affect your images. The ƒ/1.48, for example, produces a more shallow depth of field, while the ƒ/4.0 will have more of the image in focus.
Just remember that with a variable aperture, the lower the f-number, the wider the aperture and the more light reaches the sensor. That allows the camera to use a faster shutter speed in the same lighting conditions, while also producing a shallower depth of field. By contrast, the higher the f-number, the smaller the aperture, letting in less light but increasing the amount of the scene that can remain in focus. The latter can be useful for landscapes and group shots, for example.
summary: The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max introduce a major camera upgrade with a new four-stop variable aperture on the Main camera, replacing the previous fixed aperture. This feature allows the camera to physically adjust the amount of light reaching the sensor, improving low-light performance and offering optical control over the depth of field. Users can let the phone control the aperture automatically or adjust it manually through the Camera app.
key_points: The iPhone 18 Pro models feature a new four-stop variable aperture ranging from ƒ/1.48 to ƒ/4.0 on the Main camera.
The variable aperture delivers approximately 50 percent better low-light performance compared to previous models.
Users can choose between automatic aperture control or manual adjustment via the Camera app.
Lower f-numbers let in more light and create a shallower depth of field, while higher f-numbers keep more of the scene in focus.

title: Review: Control Resonant: Remedy's Tech Makes the Leap to a Wider Urban Sandbox
author: William Judd
content:
Remedy Entertainment returns with Control Resonant, marking a distinct departure from the studio's traditional linear shooter format in favour of a semi-open-world melee action title. Operating on Remedy's proprietary Northlight game engine - previously responsible for visual showcases such as Alan Wake 2 - the game pushes technical ambitions in new directions across larger playable environments.
However, adapting an engine designed primarily for tightly controlled single-player experiences to a broader urban sandbox introduces some trade-offs.
Control Resonant features rich diffuse global illumination that gives its environments a convincing, lived-in quality with minimal artifacting. The game appears to use a precalculated global illumination solution supplemented with screen-space ambient occlusion. Volumetric lighting and atmospheric particulate fog also return to convincingly render a moody New York setting. The game's action sequences also contain a lot of physics-driven mayhem, like the original Control. Here, the player can break stone structures into fractured chunks, while propelling various props through the environment.
But Control Resonant does have some visual issues, which seem to stem from the game's expanded scale. The game's cascaded shadow maps often look incoherent and artifact-ridden from distant views. Screen-space reflections prove a fine solution for specular lighting, but the reflection detail isn't preserved when on-screen details are occluded. The game's camera follows the player at considerable distance to frame brawls, but it can collide awkwardly with walls and other geometry. Image quality isn't great either on non-Pro consoles, exhibiting substantial breakup and a poor resolve on fine details.
On the base PlayStation 5, performance mode runs at an internal resolution of roughly 864p upscaled to around 1440p using FSR, delivering a generally smooth 60fps target. Framerate drops are largely confined to minor traversal stutters and heavy transparency effects during a specific boss encounter. Quality mode increases the internal resolution to approximately 1260p, providing a sharper, near-4K presentation at a stable 30fps with modestly improved shadow coherency and reflection clarity. Hardware ray tracing is absent in both modes.
Sony's PS5 Pro provides a noticeable step up in overall visual quality and stability. In performance mode, the console leverages PSSR to reconstruct an 864p internal image to a 4K display target, significantly mitigating the shimmering and aliasing artefacts seen on the base hardware. Frame-rates are also improved, maintaining smoother - though not perfect - performance in demanding encounters.
The PlayStation 5 Pro truly sets itself apart through the inclusion of hardware-accelerated ray tracing within its quality and balanced modes. Quality mode operates at roughly 1224p at 30fps, integrating ray-traced reflections across glossy city surfaces and ray-traced shadows that resolve contact detail with variable penumbras. Meanwhile, a dedicated balanced mode introduces the same ray tracing feature set at a 1080p internal resolution targeting 40fps, making it an appealing option for displays with variable refresh rate (VRR) support.
On Microsoft hardware, Xbox Series X achieves visual and performance parity with the PlayStation 5, utilising identical 864p and 1260p resolution splits across its performance and quality modes. Performance remains solid overall, with a similar performance level to PS5. Xbox Series S operates a single visual mode matching the settings and 864p resolution of the Series X performance mode, and it generally hits a steady 30fps target.
Ultimately, Control Resonant demonstrates both the flexibility and the limits of Remedy's Northlight engine as it transitions into open-world territory. While base consoles struggle with image clarity and draw distance limitations, the overall graphical presentation remains engaging. For players seeking the optimal console experience, the PlayStation 5 Pro stands out as the premier platform, successfully using advanced upscaling and ray tracing to better realise the game's high-end visual features.
summary: Remedy Entertainment's Control Resonant transitions the studio's formula into a semi-open-world melee action game using the Northlight engine. While the game delivers impressive global illumination and physics-driven combat, its expanded scale introduces visual compromises on base consoles. The PlayStation 5 Pro offers the optimal console experience through advanced upscaling and hardware-accelerated ray tracing.
key_points: Control Resonant shifts Remedy's traditional linear shooter format into a broader urban sandbox action title.
Base consoles like the standard PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X exhibit image clarity issues and shadow artifacts due to the game's expanded scale.
The Xbox Series S runs a single visual mode matching the Series X performance settings at a steady 30fps.
The PlayStation 5 Pro provides superior visual quality and stability through PSSR upscaling and hardware-accelerated ray tracing.

title: Astartes II, the Most Anticipated Warhammer 40,000 Animation Ever, Has a New Trailer and Confirmation of Key Details
author: Wesley Yin-Poole
content:
Games Workshop has released a new trailer for Astartes II, the most anticipated Warhammer 40,000 animation ever.
For the uninitiated, the original Astartes was created by superfan Syama Pedersen, who was subsequently brought into the fold to make the official sequel. Astartes is widely accepted as the greatest Warhammer 40,000 animation ever made, official or unofficial, with only Amazon’s excellent Space Marine 2 animation for the Secret Level anthology series competing with it in quality terms. Indeed, Astartes was so good that it inspired Saber Interactive’s hugely successful Space Marine 2 in terms of the look and feel of the Space Marines themselves.
During Games Workshop’s ‘Big Autumn Preview’ event, fans were treated to a new look at Astartes II, which confirms the appearance of Deathwatch and Terminators. As the company notes in a post on Warhammer Community, fans of Space Hulk will no doubt find a lot familiar here.
ASTARTES 2 teaser
Coming December
We get to follow a Deathwatch unit investigating a Space Hulk! pic.twitter.com/DgveN5yz6K
Indeed, the Space Hulk vibes come through loud and clear. We see Space Marines stomp about a dark, shadowy interior which you just know will house horrible, nightmarish things in the shadows. But the first-person shot of a corridor lit only by spotlights is the clearest sign that the much-loved tabletop game, Space Hulk, was an influence.
Also in the post, Games Workshop confirmed that Astartes II will be “significantly longer” than its predecessor, which is music to fan ears. Understandably as a single-person fan project, Astartes is on the short side.
“We knew already that this was likely to feature Deathwatch and Terminators, from the unsubtle hints dropped at the end of the LAST trailer, and now we see them, they look like they mean business,” Games Workshop said. “The imposing line of storm bolter barrels and the crackle of a power fist, combined with the ominous surroundings, are certainly giving off some strong Space Hulk vibes.
“Somehow even more intimidating than the blank visage of the Terminator helms is that unhelmeted Space Marine veteran, who could certainly be described as ‘grizzled.’ And we think we clocked at least three different characters and Chapters of Space Marines in that trailer.”
In November last year, Games Workshop revealed animation work on a monitor screen via the promo video, below, that showed a squad of Terminators appearing to protect an unnamed human soldier. This was the Inquisition-led Deathwatch Terminator squad from the debut Astartes 2 teaser in incomplete form, but we know from their pauldron chapter symbols that they’re the same as before (Retributors, Mortifactors, Scythes of The Emperor, Sons of Medusa, and Angels Vermilion).
Last year’s teaser suggested an animation on a scale and quality never-before-seen from Warhammer 40,000, with melee combat, shooting, vehicle combat, and even spaceship battles all showcased. It showed a number of Space Marine chapters in battle across varied environments, and multiple enemy races, including Tyranids, Orks, and Tau.
But it turned out that nothing in the teaser is actually in the Astartes 2 animation itself. According to a post on the Warhammer Community website: “This teaser trailer is not actually clips from the new animation, instead showing a compilation of shots that represent the former lives of the characters that will appear in the show. There’s a pretty unsubtle hint at the end as to the nature of the final story... We’ll leave you to speculate and start putting the pieces together yourselves.”
Astartes II is due out this December on Warhammer+, Games Workshop’s streaming service.
summary: Games Workshop has released a new trailer for Astartes II, confirming that the highly anticipated Warhammer 40,000 animation will premiere in December on Warhammer+. Created by Syama Pedersen, the official sequel will be significantly longer than the original and follows a Deathwatch unit investigating a Space Hulk. The trailer showcases Terminators and evokes strong similarities to the tabletop game Space Hulk.
key_points: Astartes II is scheduled to be released in December on Games Workshop's streaming service, Warhammer+.
The new trailer confirms the appearance of Deathwatch units and Terminators.
Games Workshop stated that the upcoming animation will be significantly longer than the original fan project.
The setting and atmosphere draw heavy inspiration from the tabletop game Space Hulk.

title: The real story of the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera
author: Jacob Kastrenakes
content:
It’s one of the most fascinating years in a while when it comes to iPhone camera upgrades. The big story of the iPhone 18 Pro is the variable aperture main lens, which lets you open the aperture up wider for better low light shots and make the aperture smaller for better depth of field in group photos. But all I can get anyone to talk about is the software upgrades: it turns out, they’re a lot more useful day to day than the aperture on a camera this small.
The real story of the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera
On The Vergecast: an iPhone 18 Pro camera deep dive, the state of the AI safety debate, and more.
This week on The Vergecast, David Imel and Allison Johnson are here for a deep dive into the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera. There’s a lot to explore here, from the aperture, to the camera app’s new manual controls, to the updated imaging pipeline and the improvements to ProRAW.
After that, Hayden Field is on the show to discuss the state of the AI safety debate. Concerns are still boiling over after an Anthropic researcher quit his job to warn about the dangers of AI, and any chance for policy solutions seems to have hit a dead end. We discuss whether what’s likely to happen in the interim — third-party evaluators being embedded within the big AI labs — has any teeth, and where the safety conversation goes from here.
Finally, it’s time for a Lightning Round. We discuss Waymo’s ability to call the cops, a new ereader from Boox, and a couple of tiny retro-style cameras.
If you want to learn more about any of the topics we discussed, you can check out the stories below:
summary: The iPhone 18 Pro features notable camera upgrades, highlighted by a new variable aperture main lens and useful daily software improvements like manual controls, an updated imaging pipeline, and ProRAW enhancements. A recent episode of The Vergecast discussed these camera features alongside the ongoing AI safety debate and other tech news. The podcast also covered topics such as Waymo's police-calling capabilities, a new Boox ereader, and retro-style cameras during its lightning round.
key_points: The iPhone 18 Pro introduces a variable aperture main lens for improved low-light shots and depth of field.
Software upgrades and new manual controls in the camera app prove particularly useful for daily use.
The Vergecast featured a deep dive into the iPhone 18 Pro camera, the AI safety debate, and other recent tech developments.

title: New GTA 5 Leak Suggests Rockstar Had Ambitious, City-Sized DLC Plans That Were Ultimately Scrapped
author: Wesley Yin-Poole
content:
GTA 5 has suffered a new leak that suggests Rockstar Games had ambitious, city-sized DLC plans for the game.
Reports emerging online today indicate a near 200GB version of the GTA 5 source code initially leaked in 2023 has now been made public, and interested parties are analyzing it as we speak. The highlight here is what looks like a Liberty City DLC for GTA 5 that obviously never saw the light of day (GTA Online’s enormous success steered Rockstar away from story DLC towards multiplayer focused updates).
According to X / Twitter user TJGM, the Liberty City DLC found in the files has been extrapolated and visualized to show just how much bigger this version of the city is compared to the one found in GTA 4. “Here's a look at the expanded Liberty City layout,” they tweeted. “This outline of the map is drawn based on where shorelines are, the lines indicate zones that play shoreline audio.”
There is speculation online that this Liberty City DLC may have been held back for GTA 6, but there is no evidence to suggest that is Rockstar’s plan.
More has emerged from this leak: Agent Trevor DLC mission names; cut vehicles, cut dialogue, cut cutscenes, and more on GTA 5. There also appears to be very early GTA 6 work in the files.
On Agent Trevor, GTA fans have known for some time that Rockstar worked on a single-player DLC for GTA 5 that would have seen Trevor assume the role of a secret agent. In 2024, actor Steven Ogg said Rockstar originally planned to make a story expansion focused on his character, Trevor, with it thought to have fallen by the wayside as the developer focused on the cash cow that was GTA Online.
Ogg was joined by Michael actor Ned Luke and Franklin actor Shawn Fonteno in a Questions and Answers session with Streamily, and the trio shed light on what they claimed was scrapped downloadable content for GTA 5 that starred Trevor as a Federal Investigation Bureau agent.
"Originally they were gonna do continuing stories of Michael, Franklin, and Trevor," Luke said, and Ogg expanded on his version. "We also had that really cool s**t of — and I forget if it was DLC, I have no idea — but where Trevor was gonna be undercover, he works for the FEDs," Ogg said. "And we did shoot some of that stuff with James Bond Trevor. He's still kind of a f**k up but he's doing his best. And we shot some stuff and then it just disappeared and they never followed up on it."
Also in 2024, Joe Robino, who was a senior camera artist and virtual cinematographer working at Rockstar’s New York office from 2010 to 2016, spoke to the SanInPlay YouTube channel about why the GTA 5 story DLC was canceled.
“A lot of the team went to do Red Dead Redemption 2 right away and I took on this other project that was a standalone DLC for GTA that never came out and it was kick ass,” Robino revealed.
“That was my thing. I was one of the main editors, camera artists, and on-stage stuff. We split our teams into two. I stayed on GTA Online and then this DLC, which Steven Ogg [the actor who played Trevor Philips] was a very important part of.
“And then some of the team overlapped and went to RDR2 early on, and then we just kind of did this [flipped motion], because when that game got shelved, we spent so much money… a lot of that stuff though did end up making it I believe into later iterations of GTA Online, I think. So it’s not like they wasted it.
“It was really really good. But when GTA Online came out it was so much of a cash cow and people were loving it so much that it was hard to make an argument that a standalone DLC would outcompete that. I think looking back now you could probably do both. But that was a business decision they made. I was a little upset about that.
“That actually was a lot of the reason for me being a little sour at that time. Because I was like yo, WTF guys? This s**t’s awesome. Let’s keep going. Let’s finish this s**t.”
Fans have had snippets of information about GTA 5’s fabled story DLC over the years. GTA dataminers have also discovered a reference to Trevor with a jetpack, which suggests story mode DLC was repurposed into GTA Online, as Robino said. In 2018, Rockstar finally unveiled GTA Online's Doomsday Heist missions alongside the Thruster jetpack.
Last year, speaking on the Lex Fridman podcast, Rockstar Games co-founder and former lead writer Dan Houser addressed the DLC for the first time, insisting that if the developer had continued with it, it wouldn’t have been able to make 2018’s Red Dead Redemption 2.
“The internet knows we made a DLC… single-player DLC for GTA 5 that never came out,” Houser said.
“It was one when you played as Trevor, but he was a secret agent. It was cute. It never quite came together, and it was never finished. It was about half done when it got abandoned. But I think if that had come out, we probably wouldn’t have gotten to make Red Dead 2. So, there are always compromises.”
What approach will Rockstar take with GTA 6? Will it go back to story DLC, or focus on whatever new version of GTA Online it has up its sleeve? Some think Rockstar will eventually add multiple cities, including Liberty City, to GTA 6, alongside GTA Online 2 or whatever the multiplayer mode ends up being called. For now, though, it’s a case of what might have been for GTA 5.
Last week, as part of the ongoing employment tribunal to determine the fate of the 31 GTA 6 developers Rockstar fired last year, the company revealed the extreme lengths it goes to in order to prevent security breaches.
Rockstar has suffered a string of high-profile leaks over the years, most recently the 'CyberLeek' incident which saw GTA 6 gameplay hit the internet ahead of the game's Netflix special. Speaking at the tribunal, Rockstar said it's under intense scrutiny as the developer of GTA.
“Guarding the secrets of the unique gameplay and design are akin to Apple protecting the iPhone or Coke protecting its formula,” Rockstar said, adding that it adopts “the security posture of a Wall Street bank.”
In April 2025, Rockstar dismissed an employee in Lincoln, UK, who it alleged disclosed confidential information about GTA 6 to a third party who then published the information to social media. Rockstar dismissed an employee in the U.S. in November 2023 and another in India in November 2025 for two separate acts of information leaking.
Rockstar pointed out the frequency of coffee shop trips by employees and pizza deliveries to the Rockstar offices have been monitored by fans, and traffic volumes by its workplaces were allegedly tracked in a bid to get an inside track on the GTA 6 release date.
summary: A recently leaked near-200GB version of the GTA 5 source code has revealed plans for an ambitious, city-sized Liberty City DLC that was ultimately scrapped. The files and past developer statements confirm that Rockstar shifted its focus toward GTA Online and Red Dead Redemption 2 instead of completing single-player expansions like the 'Agent Trevor' DLC. Additionally, the leaked data includes cut vehicles, dialogue, and very early work on GTA 6.
key_points: A 200GB GTA 5 source code leak made public online reveals plans for a scrapped city-sized Liberty City DLC.
Actor Steven Ogg and former Rockstar staff confirmed that a single-player DLC starring Trevor as an undercover FIB agent was partially developed before being shelved.
Former Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser stated that continuing the single-player DLC would have prevented the studio from making Red Dead Redemption 2.
Some assets from the abandoned GTA 5 story expansions were repurposed into GTA Online updates, such as the Doomsday Heist and jetpacks.

title: The Google Pixel 10a is down by nearly 50% with Giffgaff
author: Gian Estrada
content:
Google Pixel 10a only launched six months ago, and now you can get it for just £250.
Giffgaff has slashed that £519 price tag down to just £250, handing anyone who moves fast a huge £269 saving on a phone that still delivers flagship camera smarts, a beefy battery and years of software support straight out of the box.
![Google Pixel 10a on a yellow stone background](https://www.trustedreviews.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/7/2026/06/Google-Pixel-10a-on-a-yellow-stone-background-450x253.png) 
Google Pixel 10a falls to almost half price, now £250
Google Pixel 10a price falls to almost half its original cost, now down to just £250 from £519, a saving of £269.
You can see where some of that saving shows up the moment you switch it on, with the 6.3-inch pOLED display now noticeably brighter, reaching 3000 nits at its peak for HDR playback and staying easy to read in bright daylight or while streaming in bed each night.
The camera tells a similarly strong story, as our mobile editor, Lewis Painter, spent over a week testing the Google Pixel 10a as his main phone and was most impressed by a 48MP camera that delivers sharp, naturally coloured shots even in tricky, shifting light.
That same processing power carries into the phone’s AI toolkit, with Magic Editor and Best Take joining newer additions like Camera Coach to help even casual photographers get more out of every shot they take.
SQUIRREL_PLAYLIST_10148964
Powering all of that is the same Tensor G4 chipset found in last year’s model, which pairs with 8GB of RAM to handle everyday tasks and casual gaming smoothly, backed by seven years of guaranteed Android updates.
Lewis also praised the completely flat rear panel and the 5100mAh battery, noting the Google Pixel 10a comfortably lasted a full day of messaging, photos and evening plans with charge to spare. Faster 30W wired charging means a short top-up keeps it running well into the evening.
With full IP68 water resistance, a smooth 120Hz refresh rate and Gorilla Glass protection also included, the Google Pixel 10a at £250 stands out as one of the more complete mid-range phones anyone could buy this month.
Anyone weighing up a new phone this year would struggle to find better value than the Google Pixel 10a, now available at less than half its original £519 price tag while stock in either Obsidian or Lavender lasts.
![Google Pixel 10a on a table](https://www.trustedreviews.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/7/2026/03/Google-Pixel-10a-1-820x461.jpg) 
![4 Star Recommended Badge](https://www.trustedreviews.com/wp-content/themes/trusted-reviews-child/assets/badges/4-star.png) 
It’s tough to get hyped for the Pixel 10a when it’s basically a twin of the now-cheaper Pixel 9a, offering only minor tweaks like a brighter screen and a flatter back. While it’s definitely not worth the upgrade for current 9a users, it’s still a solid mid-range pick that keeps Google in the game for now.
![The Whatsapp Logo](https://www.trustedreviews.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/7/2024/11/Whatsapp-Logo-1-450x450.png)
summary: Giffgaff has reduced the price of the Google Pixel 10a from £519 to £250, offering a £269 saving just six months after its launch. The mid-range phone features a brighter 6.3-inch pOLED display, a 48MP camera, a Tensor G4 chipset, and a 5100mAh battery. While it represents minor tweaks over the previous Pixel 9a, the current discount provides exceptional value while stock lasts.
key_points: The Google Pixel 10a is available from Giffgaff for £250, down from its original £519 price.
The phone features a 6.3-inch pOLED display with a peak brightness of 3000 nits.
It is powered by the Tensor G4 chipset, paired with 8GB of RAM and a 5100mAh battery.
Key hardware includes a 48MP camera, IP68 water resistance, and a 120Hz refresh rate.
Buyers receive seven years of guaranteed Android updates.

title: Bose unveils new Ultra Open Earbuds and Sport Open Earbuds
author: Vlad
content:
Today Bose has unveiled the new Sport Open Earbuds and the Ultra Open Earbuds. Both of these are "designed to create more listening moments across active pursuits and everyday life", the company says. These second-generation Ultra Open Earbuds represent Bose's new flagship open-ear experience, while the new Sport Open Earbuds are the more affordable (yet still not cheap) option.
The Ultra Open Earbuds have a newly engineered driver that delivers deeper bass and a higher volume than the first-gen model. Snapdragon Sound support is also there, with aptX Adaptive for high-quality audio. SpeechClarity technology keeps calls clear and natural while Auto Volume adjusts to fluctuations in the environment.

Bose Ultra Open Earbuds official images
These also have Cinema Mode, powered by Bose TrueSpatial technology, which "creates a wider, more immersive soundstage while keeping dialogue sharp, clear, and precisely centered" for a "theater-like experience that works with any content source".
![More Bose Ultra Open Earbuds official images](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/09/bose-ultra-open-earbuds-sport-open-earbuds-official/popup/-x99/gsmarena_013.jpg) 
![More Bose Ultra Open Earbuds official images](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/09/bose-ultra-open-earbuds-sport-open-earbuds-official/popup/-x99/gsmarena_014.jpg) 
![More Bose Ultra Open Earbuds official images](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/09/bose-ultra-open-earbuds-sport-open-earbuds-official/popup/-x99/gsmarena_015.jpg)

![More Bose Ultra Open Earbuds official images](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/09/bose-ultra-open-earbuds-sport-open-earbuds-official/popup/-x99/gsmarena_017.jpg) 
![More Bose Ultra Open Earbuds official images](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/09/bose-ultra-open-earbuds-sport-open-earbuds-official/popup/-x99/gsmarena_018.jpg) 
More Bose Ultra Open Earbuds official images
The new Ultra Open Earbuds have a "refined metallic cap with a beveled finish" and a redesigned case that can stand upright and supports wireless charging. Battery life is up to 9 hours on the buds, and the case provides an additional 19.5 hours of charge.
The new Sport Open Earbuds are "built for running, fitness, and a wide range of outdoor activities", prioritizing stability, comfort, and durability, with textured physical buttons. They have custom-designed dynamic drivers that deliver "full, balanced audio". These support Auto Volume too.
![Bose Sport Open Earbuds](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/09/bose-ultra-open-earbuds-sport-open-earbuds-official/popup/-x99/gsmarena_001.jpg) 
![Bose Sport Open Earbuds](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/09/bose-ultra-open-earbuds-sport-open-earbuds-official/popup/-x99/gsmarena_002.jpg) 
![Bose Sport Open Earbuds](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/09/bose-ultra-open-earbuds-sport-open-earbuds-official/popup/-x99/gsmarena_003.jpg) 
![Bose Sport Open Earbuds](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/09/bose-ultra-open-earbuds-sport-open-earbuds-official/popup/-x99/gsmarena_004.jpg) 
![Bose Sport Open Earbuds](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/09/bose-ultra-open-earbuds-sport-open-earbuds-official/popup/-x99/gsmarena_005.jpg) 
![Bose Sport Open Earbuds](https://fdn.gsmarena.com/imgroot/news/26/09/bose-ultra-open-earbuds-sport-open-earbuds-official/popup/-x99/gsmarena_006.jpg) 
Bose Sport Open Earbuds
Their design ensures that they stay put during head shakes, cartwheels, and "other activity bound to put a secure fit to the ultimate test", Bose says. They are IP54 rated for dust, sweat, and splash resistance, and the silicone construction is "built to withstand the demands of activity while making dirt and grime easy to wipe away". The charging case stands upright and supports wireless charging.
The Sport Open Earbuds have up to 7 hours of battery life, with up to 22 additional hours of charge from the case. Both the Ultra Open Earbuds and the Sport Open Earbuds use Bluetooth 5.4 and support multipoint connectivity with two devices, as well as Google Fast Pair. Each of them has the option for customizable shortcuts for Spotify Tap and quick access to your phone's voice assistant.
The Sport Open Earbuds are priced at $199, while the Ultra Open Earbuds cost $299. They will both become available on October 1, with pre-orders starting on September 19. At some point after the launch, Bose promises to deliver a firmware update that will enable support for Google Find Hub, Alexa+, and shortcut support for Apple Music. The Bose app has an adjustable three-band EQ, as well as settings for Auto Volume control.
summary: Bose has announced the second-generation Ultra Open Earbuds and the new Sport Open Earbuds, both designed for active pursuits and everyday use. The flagship Ultra Open model features upgraded drivers, Snapdragon Sound support, and Cinema Mode, priced at $299. Meanwhile, the more affordable Sport Open Earbuds cost $199 and prioritize stability, durability, and fitness tracking with an IP54 rating. Both models launch on October 1 with pre-orders beginning September 19, featuring Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint connectivity, and wireless charging cases.
key_points: Bose unveiled the second-generation Ultra Open Earbuds ($299) and the new Sport Open Earbuds ($199).
The Ultra Open Earbuds offer up to 9 hours of battery life with an extra 19.5 hours from the wireless charging case.
The Sport Open Earbuds are IP54 rated for dust, sweat, and splash resistance, offering up to 7 hours of battery life.
Both earbuds feature Bluetooth 5.4, Google Fast Pair, multipoint connectivity, and customizable shortcuts.
Pre-orders begin on September 19, and the products will become available on October 1.

title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 In-Depth Review: Does it Match the Hype?
author: Ray Maker
content:
![Youtube video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/rrY6nDE7ukk/hqdefault.jpg)
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is arguably the biggest internal update the Apple Watch has seen in a number of years, and certainly the biggest Apple Watch Ultra series update since launch. It has a far better optical heart rate sensor than in the past, new audio intelligence features, and even a brand-new Readiness score system built atop all of that. Plus, there are promises of further new features later this year with a new Apple Health app that’s consumer-friendly, as well as more audio intelligence features.
But probably the most notable thing about both the Ultra 4 and the new Series 12 (which both my wife and I are also testing) is that new optical HR sensor, which is backed by an Apple study involving 1,400 people, including the majority of whom were dual-wristing other competitor watches. In this post (and the above video), I’m going to dive into some of those claims in that Apple-backed paper, and most critically, whether they stand up to real-life scrutiny out on the road (and trails, and gyms).
With that, let’s dive into it!
What’s New:
![IMG_5441.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_5441.jpg)
There’s a lot new in this unit, and I’m going to cover virtually all the new features throughout this review. But if you’re looking for the quick and dirty, here’s everything that’s new on the Apple Watch Ultra 4, compared to the previous Apple Watch Ultra 3:
Apple Watch Ultra 4 Hardware Updates/Changes:
– Gets new S11 chipset, which has features from the new A20 Pro chips of the iPhone 18 Pro
– Gets new secure audio processing exclave within that (for Audio Intelligence)
– Ultra 4 increased battery life to “over 2 days” (50 hours, technically)
– Ultra 4 adds revamped ‘Extended Battery’ (GPS) mode and new ‘Max Extended Mode’ (GPS workout battery life of 45 hours, without reducing either GPS or recorded HR data
– Boatloads of new bands for all of them, including new translucent Ocean bands on the Ultra
– Ultra 4 offered in same two core colors (black or silver)
Apple Watch Heart Rate Sensing Hardware Update:
– New heart rate sensor with increased electrode surface area for better ECGs
– New photodiodes below it for better workout capture
– New LED array below that for better 24×7 HR readings
– New HR sensor is thinner (bump) than in the past
– Increased background (non-workout) HR readings to every 5 seconds (60x more than before)
– Increased HRV readings to every 5 minutes (24x more than before)
– Claim of Apple Watch Series 12/Ultra 4 “Most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable”
– Published their own white paper to support that claim, with competitor comparisons
New HRV Features:
– Added overnight HRV trending/recording within the Vitals app (as one of key metrics)
– Added new HRV into new ‘Daytime’ view in the Vitals app
– Requires 7 nights of initial data on a watch to get HRV trends in the Vitals app
New Readiness Score Feature:
– Each morning you’ll get a new score
– Score is based on a range of 0-10 (zero being worst, 10 being highest)
– Four core descriptors you can get: Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, Go For It
– Can be viewed on the watch or the Fitness App
– Leverages your Sleep data, Vitals Metrics, Training Load, and recent Activity data
– Requires 7 nights of initial data for the HRV trends, before it can populate Readiness Scores.
New Health App Redesign (on phone, coming later this year):
– Adds new AI summary and recommendations
– Adds Apple Intelligence guidance, including suggesting intervals
– Adds new Health Age: Based on Sleep, VO2Max, HRV, Heart Rate, Exercise Minutes, Steps, and optionally Labs
– Adds new longevity Tab, based on Nutrition, Metabolic, Overall Movement, Sleep, Hearing, Heart metrics, mental wellbeing
– Adds support for pulling in lab work
– Adds new VO2Max test (test can be done in living room in 6 minutes)
– Adds new other tests for flexibility, movement mechanics, strength, and more, which can be trended.
– Health app coming later this year in beta in English
New Audio Intelligence features (on-device, some features later this year):
– Everything done on-device, without need for your phone (at least for immediate processing)
– [Available today] Adds Sound Recognition alerts for sirens, doorbells, baby crying, and more (shows up as text on watch)
– [Available today] Instant Shazam: Will instantly show you the name of songs when you raise your wrist
– [Available later 2026] Live Rewind: Double-tap the Digital Crown to get a text-only transcription of the last 15 seconds of spoken words
– [Available later 2026] Siri Recap: Will summarize conversations/spoken words heard around you into a recap that’s available on your phone.
– Can configure all features independently (enabled/disabled, plus further focus-mode-like controls for Siri Recap)
Got all that? Phew, let’s get right into the daily usage bits.
Daily Usage Basics:
![IMG_6297.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6297.jpg)
In this section I’m going to dive into the daily basics of the watch – mostly from a health and activity tracking perspective. Obviously, given the wide-ranging capabilities of the Apple Watch as a smartwatch, there’s far more that I’m not going to cover here (such as music storage/playback, contactless payments, 3rd-party apps, etc…). These largely haven’t changed this time around, save for the handful of new Audio Intelligence features that I mention later in the review.
With that, the first thing you probably already know is that the Apple Watch Ultra 4 requires an iPhone be paired with it. It’s unable to pair to an Android phone, and needs an iPhone 11 or newer (it needs an iPhone capable of running iOS27, full list here). In turn, for Apple Intelligence-related features, it needs an iPhone from that list (basically an iPhone 15 Pro, or 16/17/18 anything). Said differently, if you’ve bought an iPhone in the last few years you’re probably good, but if you’ve got something distinctly older, you might be limited on features (or not work at all).
As for the watch hardware, the externals of the Apple Watch Ultra 4 haven’t changed any since last year (save for the heart rate sensor on the back I’ll discuss in a moment). It’s still the same 1.98” screen capable of up to 3,000 nits of peak brightness. I’ve had no issues seeing that screen in bright conditions, or inversely, no issues with it being too bright in dark conditions (it’s capable of dropping down to a tiny 1 nit of brightness at night). In the case below, out on the sea…albeit with not exactly the correct sports profile to track it…but hey, it worked.
![IMG_5718.jpeg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_5718.jpeg)
On the side of the Ultra 4 you’ve got three buttons. The left side has the Action Button, which is unique within the Apple Watch lineup to just the Ultra series. This button is customizable, though in my configuration it opens up the workout app, and then once that app is opened and a workout started, it’ll act as a lap button. Again, you can choose which app to leverage, and then what you want it to do within that app.
![IMG_6299 2.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6299-2.jpg)

Readiness Score & Vitals:
![IMG_6294 2.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6294-2.jpg)
Now normally (and in the future), I’d likely just blend the Readiness Score & Vitals sections into either the Daily Basics or Sports sections, but given it’s new this year (for Readiness, and expanded Vitals), I’m gonna pull it out into its own section to make it a bit more detailed.
Apple’s new Readiness Score is effectively competing with readiness scores from Google/Fitbit, Garmin, and, to a slightly lesser extent, Whoop & Oura (those last two don’t really have the same type of dynamic and singular scores that Google or Garmin do). The score starts off with having two key components: A numerical value and a descriptor. The numerical value is from 0-10 (with zero being the worst, and 10 being the highest). And then within that, there are four descriptors you can get. Here’s an example of my score yesterday about 90 minutes after I woke up (it’ll change dynamically through the day, as I’ll show, though it hadn’t changed yet here):
![IMG_5889.jpeg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_5889.jpeg)
You can see my score was a ‘7’, with a descriptor of ‘Ready’. Here’s a quick look at the descriptors available, and their corresponding ranges:
![ReadinessScores.png](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/ReadinessScores.png)
Or, numerically:
– 0-1: Recover
– 2-4: Pace Yourself
– 5-7: Ready
– 8-10: Go for it
These scores are in turn based on four core umbrella categories:
– Fitness: This is primarily your workouts, but can also include other activity
– Overnight Vitals: This includes your overnight resting heart rate, respiration rate, wrist temperature, and overnight HRV
– Daylight Vitals: This includes your resting heart rate during the day, and HRV during the day
– Sleep Score: This is your sleep score from last night, based on sleep times/durations/phases
Getting a readiness score requires some historical data. The longest period is 7 nights’ worth of HRV data before your first Readiness Score will populate, which is done on a per-watch basis. Likewise, other per-watch metrics include your wrist temperature. As well as your resting heart rate and respiration rate. Point being, it’ll be 7 nights’ worth of days (with a minimum of 4 hours of sleep per night), before you get a score. Finally, your data is then trended against a 49-day historical span (7 weeks). Apple says they found that the right balance is using historical data as a counterweight, versus being too long to not track recent fitness gains.
Now, as noted, your score is dynamic throughout the day. That’s similar to Garmin’s Readiness score, which is dynamic throughout the day, whereas Google/Fitbit’s readiness score is not dynamic throughout the day. So fast-forward a few hours later, and around 1PM I went out for a 2-hour-long road cycling ride:
![GX013299_still.jpeg GX013299 still.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/GX013299_still.jpeg)
This ride was of medium intensity. Nothing too crazy. Upon returning and saving my ride, the watch immediately notified me that my Readiness score had dropped down to 5 – still ‘Ready’ (from 7). That makes sense, as my ‘readiness’ to train or tackle additional load was now lower. Inversely, had this not been crazy-busy watch review season and I somehow had time to take a nap, that score could then improve a few hours later (perhaps to 6 from 5).
![IMG_6038 2.jpeg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6038-2-1.jpeg)
Now, fast forward again another few hours later, and it was time for a group track session under the lights. In this case, my readiness score was still 5 at the start of the session.
![IMG_6148.jpeg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6148-1.jpeg)
An hour later of 8x600m repeats at a reasonably strong pace, I saved my workout. Initially, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 didn’t update my Readiness score. Whereas the Series 12 worn on the other wrist immediately updated it to 3 (Pace Yourself). However, about two hours after I completed the run, the Ultra 4 finally updated its score to a ‘3’ as well, as seen below:
![IMG_6202.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6202.jpg)
It was a bit odd that it took so long to show up, but it’s also a pattern I’ve seen with the Series 12 (both are paired to different phones, though they do share the same backend account). For example, the Series 12 showed my sleep score immediately on my phone, but refused for 4 hours to show the sleep score on the watch, and thus no readiness score. Then magically, it showed both. Likewise, I often get null results (as seen below), only for it to update seconds later, or show an entirely different incorrect value for a few seconds before correcting.
![IMG_6196 2.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6196-2.jpg)
Point is, there seem to be some minor ‘speed’/display bugs to work out there. Apple says they’re working on it, and hope to have fixes shortly.
Now of course, these scores are still ‘early days’ for Readiness. I’ve only got a few days of Readiness scores as of this writing. And in fact, the Daytime HRV value trending still hasn’t shown up (I get daily values, but not yet trending). Apparently, that is a bit more picky on how it establishes that trend, despite now having 8 days of data on it. I’m not terribly sure what to do with the Daytime HRV values anyways. Huawei semi-recently started adding that on some models, but otherwise, nobody else shows consumers daytime HRV values. This is probably because they are incredibly variable minute to minute and hour to hour in a non-resting state. I’m honestly a bit surprised that Apple went down the path of exposing them, but…here we are.
![IMG_6210 3.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6210-3.jpg)
The key thing to understand here is that Apple is actually comparing to your historical values for that given time slice of the day. And those historical values exclude any periods of movement or workouts. In other words, for an active person it may take far longer to build-up a daytime HRV baseline, because you’ll get very few (if any) daytime HRV data points. For example, take a look at my data points here, and focus on the ones roughly between 9AM and 11PM. In some cases for certain days, I have zero values for a given hour time slice (e.g., 2-3PM).
![IMG_6244.PNG](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6244.png) 
![IMG_6245.PNG](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6245.png) 
![IMG_6247.PNG](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6247.png)
Thus, I have to keep waiting until my ‘hourly’ cup is full for a period of 7 days for each hour of the day to see the recovery HRV value during that time period. Further, it means I could see a trended vitals value from 4-5PM, but not 2-3PM. Apple says they’re doing this to ensure the data better maps to your circadian rhythm. I get the thinking here, but this just seems really complicated, in a very not-Apple-like-way.
Oh, you can also see your daytime HRV values in the revamped Heart app on the Apple Watch, for example, this: here at the end of my day:
![IMG_6190_still.jpeg IMG 6190 still.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6190_still.jpeg)
Now, as for the nighttime HRV values, Apple says it does a simple average of the in-sleep values for the night. This is great, and adheres to the industry norms of what others do. Further, Apple uses RMSSD for their nightly/recovery HRV values (and all values shown in Vitals), again, letting you compare it with others.
![IMG_6204 3.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6204-3.jpg)
Whereas for the previous value type of SDNN, Apple says it’ll still use that for irregular rhythm notifications, an input to the Health Age feature coming in the new app, as well as some other features.
Finally, to round things out, as noted, Readiness depends on the Vitals scores that you’ve seen previously (launched previously), just with HRV added in there. Here’s how that looks each day:
![IMG_6201.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6201.jpg)
If you have an outlier (as defined as a comparison to your personal historic baseline), then it’ll turn pink. If you have multiple outliers, it’ll also push a notification to you to be aware of it. These outliers can and will also drag down your Readiness score. In fact, when it comes to ‘why’ your Readiness score is lower, you can see that both within the watch, as well as the ‘Readiness’ chunk in the Fitness app (and eventually the new Apple Health app). Here are some examples throughout the day as it changed:
![IMG_0933.PNG](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_0933-1.png) 
![IMG_6175.PNG](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6175.png) 
![IMG_6185 2.PNG](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6185-2.png)
Overall, I think Apple’s Readiness implementation is pretty solid. It roughly follows what others have done, and does so in an equally easy way to understand. Very Apple-like. Though, I’m hoping the delays are merely a one-off fluke. That said, I’ll be revisiting this in a week or two with some thoughts on how the Readiness Scores compare to others. For example, last night after the track workout, you can see how these two aligned. I’d argue the truth is probably halfway in between here.
![IMG_6227 4.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6227-4.jpg)
In this case, keep in mind that Garmin has *far* more HRV data in my account than Apple does, since Apple merely has 7 nights’ worth (and Garmin has years). Further, Apple doesn’t let you leverage different-watch data in these trends. So in my case, all my years of Apple Watch data is mostly irrelevant when I switched to the Ultra 4. Whereas again, Garmin has years of data (but only leverages the last 90 days). So it’s likely to have a bit of a house advantage in the short term. Still, there is no industry standard for how to define a Readiness score; it’s up to each company. Ultimately, a gut check is still required. But again, more down the road.
Sports Tracking:
![IMG_6315.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6315.jpg)
The Apple Watch Ultra series is quite a capable sports watch, depending on how you plan to use it. I’ve used it without issue in the past with the Ultra 3 for long 15-hour single-day treks 70KM into the mountains. And then with the Ultra 4, across numerous sports. Sure, it won’t have quite the depth of sports information as a Garmin Fenix series watch (especially when it comes to navigation/mapping), but if you don’t plan to get lost in the woods, then the Ultra 4 will likely cover you just fine.
To begin, you’ll open up the Workout app. That app can be accessed via the Action Button (assuming you’ve configured it in a default setting), allowing you to select a sport type. Apple has a huge list of sport types (here’s the full list). In general, the key difference between Apple and something like a Garmin/COROS/Amazfit/Suunto/etc…is that Apple will distill all cycling down to ‘Outdoor Cycle’, whereas the others will have separate sport profiles for Road Cycling, Mountain Biking, Gravel Cycling, eBike, eMTB, etc… Same goes for running just being ‘Outdoor Run’ versus others having Trail Run, Track Run, Adventure Run, etc…
In any case, while Apple announced new sport modes last year with the Ultra 3/Series 11, there are no new sport modes this year on the Ultra 4/Series 12.
![IMG_6316.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6316.jpg)
Once you’ve selected a sports mode, you’ll see in the upper corners that there are four ways to get into additional settings/features (shown above):
Upper left: Workout Views (aka your data pages/settings)
Upper right: Workout goals & structured workouts (aka the different ways you can have the watch tell you to suffer), including the new Extended and Max Extended modes
Lower left: Music (all things music)
Lower right: Workout Buddy & Voice Alerts (thus, all things voice-over related)
You can customize your data fields (called ‘Workout Views’), within the watch, selecting the data fields you want. Again, there’s a reasonable level of customization here, but you can’t go super-crazy with lots of hyper-specific endurance sports data fields. It’s a balance. More than Google, but less than Garmin.
![IMG_6317.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6317.jpg) 
![IMG_6318.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6318.jpg)
There’s also the ability to do structured workouts, which can be created on the phone, or pushed from platforms like TrainingPeaks, Strava/Runna, and more:
![IMG_6319.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6319.jpg)
One of the new features of the Ultra 4/Series 12 is the new Extended and Max Extended modes:
![IMG_6320.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6320.jpg) 
![IMG_6321.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6321.jpg)
This extends out the GPS battery for the Ultra 4 from 20 hours to 25 hours in ‘Extended’ mode, whereas the ‘Max Extended’ mode gets you 45 hours of GPS battery time. Here are the trade-offs:
Extended mode (25 hours GPS): Retains everything but turns off always on display, and running form metrics turned off. Cellular operations gets batches a bit. Everything else remains on, this is effectively the previous ‘Low Power Mode’ renamed.
Max extended mode (45 hours GPS): Retains 1-second GPS update rate (with dual/multi-band satellites), HR data recorded at every 5 seconds like normal, but showing a 5 minute rolling average on screen instead of instant updates. No splits, no alerts, no custom workouts. Plus previously cellular batching, no running metrics, and display not always-on.
In any case, with all that sorted, once you start the workout, it’ll show your data pages as normal (assuming a normal configuration). There’s nothing really unique here for the Ultra 4 compared to the past. Here’s an example of some data fields:
One slightly notable thing is that Workout Buddy (which was introduced last year) will audibly tell you about your Readiness Score within the intro to each workout. Or at least, all my workouts thus far. Still, as with the past, I find it frequently hallucinates about the things it says, even over the past week. Both making up things that don’t exist and just saying downright weird stuff (phrasing especially). That said, on the whole I don’t mind it, and have learned to kinda treat it like the tipsy uncle at the wedding party. Usually entertaining, even if he says some downright wonky things. Of course, you can still turn it off if you don’t like it.
When it comes to post-workout stats, Apple has a pretty brief list on the watch itself. Nothing fancy here:
Though, you can get slightly more data in the Apple Fitness app on your phone, and see/re-arrange stats. The track workout map is a little wonky here because we were actually going on/off track in between some intervals.
One of the stats you’ll see is your training load. Within the Apple realm, training load is a combination of the duration of your workout, and the Effort Rating you give it. At the end of every workout, it’ll ask you to rate your suffering, such as this:
![IMG_6324.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6324.jpg)
When you do so, it’ll feed into the overall Training Load that Apple has, and trends against your historical norms. This means that it’s a bit more subjective than other companies, which have a specific algorithm tied to heart rate (usually).
![IMG_6323.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_6323.jpg)
The downside to this is that you may not be a great judge of your effort (or specifically, how to compare a short intense track workout vs a longer duration easy run). But inversely, this ‘solves’ for the problem of dealing with really long but relatively low-heart-rate efforts (like a 15-hour trek). In the case of Garmin/etc… those tend to be given very low training load values (even less than a 5-10KM run), since the heart rates tend to be lower. Yet, those longer 12-15 hour efforts often have far greater strain on your body than a 5-10KM run.
Realistically though, if data is your jam, you’ll still probably find Apple’s Fitness app pretty thin on stats, analysis, or even the ability to dig /zoom deeper into things like heart rate charts. This area could use some love. Thankfully, there are plenty of apps that are out there, which can easily tap into the Apple Health data (via HealthKit), and slice and dice your data any number of ways.
As I’ve said before, one of my favorites continues to be HealthFit, which I use for syncing data to numerous data platforms (including any moment now the DCR Analyzer), but also tons of other platforms. And then beyond that, it has tons of ways to analyze your data.

Likewise, when it comes to navigation and routing, you’re almost certainly going to need a 3rd-party app if you’re doing anything even mildly complicated (or, if you live outside the US). I wrote a bunch about this last year in the Ultra 3 review, and none of it has changed here either. GPS & Heart Rate Accuracy:
![AppleWatch-Ultra4-Final-Review.jpg AppleWatch Ultra4 Final Review.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/AppleWatch-Ultra4-Final-Review.jpg)
The Apple Watch Ultra has a new optical HR sensor, which includes both new hardware and new software features that I’ve outlined earlier (like the frequent HRV updates and now-5-second background HR update frequency). Here’s the quick recap on those features:
– New heart rate sensor with increased electrode surface area for better ECGs
– New photodiodes below it for better workout capture
– New LED array below that for better 24×7 HR readings
– New HR sensor is thinner (bump) than in the past
– Increased background (non-workout) HR readings to every 5 seconds (60x more than before)
– Increased HRV readings to every 5 minutes (24x more than before)
– Claim of Apple Watch Series 12/Ultra 4 “Most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable”
– Published their own white paper to support that claim, with competitor comparisons
But the better question is whether or not that accuracy paper/study represents the real-world testing I saw, and if not, why not?
I dive into this in the video quite a bit, and will probably expand it out into a separate post. But the key thing to understand is that the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Series 12 only have an update frequency during workouts of “on average” every 5 seconds within a workout. It can be every second, or every 3 seconds, or every 5 seconds…but it can also have gaps of 20 seconds. All of that depends on whether or not the HR sensor algorithm decides it has enough quality confidence to plot that data point. If not, it simply skips it.
Think of it like this illustration as a timeline (this is just something I quickly whipped up to show you how it works after multiple discussions with Apple):
![Presentation1.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/Presentation1.jpg)
From there, Apple will throw away anything that doesn’t meet its quality confidence level, thus leaving you with something like this:
![Presentation2.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/Presentation2.jpg)
Now remember that all other wearables simply always plot a data point every second, including every one of the competitors in Apple’s study. Further, in Apple’s study they *only compared the exact data timestamps from their file, to the reference Polar H10 device”. Meaning, using the example above, they only compared the values for the green dots. Not all the missing timestamps.
And as you’ll see, Apple has a lot of missing timestamps, especially when it’s unsure. So, rather than give you the wrong answer, it simply gives you no answer at all. And from a study grading standpoint, it was designed such that “no answer” = “the correct answer”. Which…ummm…is very slanted towards Apple, to say the least.
But setting aside Apple’s lopsided study, let’s look at the actual accuracy of the data. Because, to be fair, it’s very good. Is it better than its best competitors? Probably not; it seems about the same. But again, it’s really good.
First up, a relatively steady trail run:
![HR-Trailrun-Wide.png HR Trailrun Wide.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-Trailrun-Wide.png)
At a high level, this looks very, very good. No major concerns here. But of course, when we zoom in, we’ll find countless examples of sub-5-second gaps, and other gaps like this one here for 11 seconds. In this case, the Apple Watch is factually wrong – both with the gap and without the gap. Remember, in the study scenario, it wouldn’t have been docked points for this, because it didn’t plot a point.
![HR-Trailrun-Zoomed1.png HR Trailrun Zoomed1.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-Trailrun-Zoomed1.png)
Next, what about a Peloton bike ride, with some solid intervals in there? Again, at a high level, this looks really good:
![HR-PelotonWide.png HR PelotonWide.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-PelotonWide.png)
And indeed, it is good. Except there’s still plenty of gaps here, like this 12-second one. And of course, on the watch itself, it’s also only opening the heart rate display every 5 seconds (regardless of data points). So any fast-moving intervals will be wrong 80% of the time on the display.
![HR-PelotonZoomed.png HR PelotonZoomed.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-PelotonZoomed.png)
Perhaps some rowing is next? Again, at a high level things look really strong – save for that one moment we see around the 8-minute marker that it hiccups:
![HR-RowingWide.png HR RowingWide.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-RowingWide.png)
And that moment is a whole combination of errors. First it skyrockets upwards incorrectly, and then it flat-lines with a 14-second gap (when Apple probably realizes it’s wrong and goes silent), then it tries to correct and takes another 10-15 seconds to get back to being correct.
![HR-RowingZoom1.png HR RowingZoom1.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-RowingZoom1.png)
And again, we can do this all day long. Here are some 10x400m running intervals, which look very strong at a high level
![HR-Intervals400m-Wide.png HR Intervals400m Wide.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-Intervals400m-Wide.png)
Zoomed in, it’s still strong, but also with a number of gaps in there, sometimes shorter here, but certainly present:
![HR-Intervals-Zoomed.png HR Intervals Zoomed.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-Intervals-Zoomed.png)
Or this track run (8x600m), which looks fairly reasonable at a high level:
![HR-TrackRun-Wide.png HR TrackRun Wide.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-TrackRun-Wide.png)
But once we zoom in, we see numerous moments where there’s ‘normal’ ramp rate separation for optical heart rate sensors:
![HR-TrackRun-Zoomed.png HR TrackRun Zoomed.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-TrackRun-Zoomed.png)
But also some heart rate spikes, such as this:
![HR-TrackRun-Zoomed2.png HR TrackRun Zoomed2.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-TrackRun-Zoomed2.png)
And finally, an outdoor ride of a few hours. Again, at a high level this looks really good. Like, really really good. Exceptionally good, in fact:
![HR-RoadRide-Wide.png HR RoadRide Wide.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-RoadRide-Wide.png)
And had it not been for Apple’s study, I probably wouldn’t have over-thought it. But with the claims there, it’s hard to ignore moments like this:
![HR-RoadRide-Zoomed1.png HR RoadRide Zoomed1.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-RoadRide-Zoomed1.png)
Or these:
![HR-RoadRide-Zoomed2.png HR RoadRide Zoomed2.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-RoadRide-Zoomed2.png)
And these:
![HR-RoadRide-Zoomed3.png HR RoadRide Zoomed3.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/HR-RoadRide-Zoomed3.png)
Again – I think overall Apple’s delivering on a world-class optical heart rate sensor. And I fully understand their thinking of ‘not recording data points that don’t have a good confidence level’. I’m OK with that. Really, I am. But it seems disingenuous to then judge everyone else on a full data set, while Apple gets to ignore the ‘hard parts’ it can’t be sure of.
Meanwhile, when it comes to GPS accuracy, things are nearly identical to previous, though there is one minor change. Apple has confirmed that GLONASS is no longer part of the constellations that the Apple Watch Ultra 4 will leverage. They said it should have no impact on accuracy, and based on what I see, that’s the case. This follows a trend with other companies removing it as well, given the increased satellite availability of the Galileo constellation, among others.
In any case, as for GPS accuracy, let’s quickly look at a few workouts. This is one of the sets of intervals I did around and around and around, and indeed, the Ultra (and others) was very good here:
![GPS-IntervalLoopsZoomed.png GPS IntervalLoopsZoomed.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/GPS-IntervalLoopsZoomed.png)
Looking at this trail run next, at a wide/high level, everything looks quite good.
![GPS-RoadRide-Wide.png GPS RoadRide Wide.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/GPS-RoadRide-Wide.png)
Once in the trails, we can see that the Ultra 4 & Fenix 9 are very close to each other, though the Series 12 isn’t quite as accurate (it lacks multiband):
![GPS-TrailRunZoom1.png GPS TrailRunZoom1.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/GPS-TrailRunZoom1.png)
We see this in a number of places, where the Ultra 4 & Fenix 9 are very close to being perfect/are perfect:
![GPS-TrailRunZoom3.png GPS TrailRunZoom3.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/GPS-TrailRunZoom3.png)
Still, there are a handful of very brief moments where the Fenix 9 outperforms it, getting my exact placement/position correctly here, and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 (and Series 12) was just slightly off (but only a couple of meters):
![GPS-TrailRunZoom2.png GPS TrailRunZoom2.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/GPS-TrailRunZoom2.png)
Meanwhile, on road cycling up in the mountains, things were pretty good. Here’s the high-level map:
![GPS-RoadRide-Wide.png GPS RoadRide Wide.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/GPS-RoadRide-Wide-1.png)
And then, zooming in to these switchbacks, you can see things look fairly close between them, with a little bit more perfection from the Ultra 4 over the Series 12:
![GPS-RoadRide-Turns.png GPS RoadRide Turns.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/GPS-RoadRide-Turns.png)
Though zoomed in further to this switchback, it’s hard to decide which one is most correct. They’re all good enough here:
![GPS-RoadRide-Turns2.png GPS RoadRide Turns2.](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/GPS-RoadRide-Turns2.png)
Ultimately, for GPS accuracy of the Apple Watch Ultra 4, I don’t see any meaningful change here (negative or positive) over the Ultra 3, which was largely perfectly fine across the board.
Wrap-Up:
![IMG_5440.jpg](https://media.dcrainmaker.com/images/2026/09/IMG_5440.jpg)
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a solid upgrade for earlier Apple Watch Ultra series owners, especially the Apple Watch Ultra 1 that got left behind on the WatchOS 27 train this year. Likewise, for those wanting more battery life than a conventional Apple Watch (non-Ultra), this delivers on that. The optical HR sensor is definitely the best Apple has ever made, and the results you see above in the heart rate accuracy section certainly show that. Whether or not it’s 1bpm better than their competitors, as Apple’s study suggests, is a bit harder to support. The reality is they just aren’t comparing the same data points equally, and thus making that claim in real life is quite challenging. I would agree it’s better than most sensors out there though.
As for the new Readiness features, I’m pretty happy with what Apple delivered here. Having a dynamic score throughout the day is critical, and a piece that both Whoop & Google/Fitbit are missing. Apple’s implementation is fairly close to the broad strokes of what Garmin has, though Garmin’s tends to be a bit more responsive at this point. Perhaps once Apple sorts out their initial teething bugs around disappearing readiness values, it’ll be fairly similar. My limited results thus far show both values to be reasonably similar in overall score average. But again, more longer term data is needed there.
Finally, as for the audio intelligence features, at this point the two features they have launched with will be appreciated. The instant Shazam trick is pretty good, and for those needing a hearing assistant, the sound recognition pieces should be handy. Both do seem to have occasional quirks, but neither seems like a show-stopper at this point.
Overall, I suspect the Ultra 4 will become one of the two watches that stays on my wrists year round, replacing the Ultra 3 that sat there over the past year. With that, thanks for reading!
