title: Bose’s next open earbuds have more bass, more volume, and more battery life
author: Andrew Liszewski
content:
Bose announced a new version of its Ultra Open Earbuds that helped kick off the industry trend of clip-on wireless earbuds nearly two-and-a-half years ago. The new Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) feature a subtle redesign with improved performance in both sound quality and battery life. They’re also joined by a new cheaper alternative called the Bose Sport Open Earbuds designed to provide a more secure and stable fit during physical activities.
Bose’s next open earbuds have more bass, more volume, and more battery life
The second-gen Ultra Open Earbuds are joined by a new sport option providing a more secure fit when you’re active.
![bose1](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/bose1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0.02498750624688%2C100%2C99.950024987506&w=2400)
![bose1](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/bose1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0.02498750624688%2C100%2C99.950024987506&w=2400)
The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) will be available for preorder on September 19th for $299 with availability starting on October 1st. Color options include black, white smoke, cherry chocolate, olive green, and sky pink. Preorders and availability for the Bose Sport Open Earbuds are the same, but they’re $100 cheaper at $199. Colors include black, white smoke, and eucalyptus green.
![The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) in white against a gray background.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/bose2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
Like the original version, the new Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) feature a design that clips to your outer ear with a transducer that directs audio into your ear canal with “minimal sound leakage,” Bose claims. There’s still no ANC because these are designed to do the exact opposite and let you hear what’s going on around you while enjoying music or a podcast.
In addition to a refreshed design with a new beveled finish on each earbud’s metal cap, the 2nd Gen feature a new driver delivering higher volume with automatic adjustments and deeper bass. A new Cinema Mode simulates a “wider, more immersive soundstage” using Bose’s TrueSpatial technology while keeping dialogue clear and centered. Battery life with the buds alone has been boosted to up to nine hours (from seven hours) with an additional 19.5 hours of playback from the redesigned case that can now stand upright for use on a wireless charger.
![The Bose Sport Open Earbuds in white and green against a gray background.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/bose4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
The Bose Sport Open Earbuds take a similar approach with a design that clips to your ear to project sounds inward, but they feature a thinner cuff with a “soft silicone matte finish” providing more grip to keep them in place. Bose says the Sport version will stay secure during head shakes, cartwheels, and running. They also feature automatic volume adjustments that adapt to ambient noise levels to ensure what you’re listening to isn’t drowned out, and the customizable shortcut button on the end of each battery barrel has an added texture, so they’re easier to find while working out. Battery life is rated at up to seven hours of playback plus an additional 22 hours with the wireless charging case.
summary: Bose has announced the Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen), featuring a subtle redesign with improved sound quality, deeper bass, higher volume, and a longer battery life of up to nine hours. They are accompanied by a new, more affordable sport alternative designed for a secure fit during physical activities. Both models are available for preorder starting September 19th and will launch on October 1st.
key_points: The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) cost $299 and feature enhanced bass, higher volume, and a new Cinema Mode.
Battery life for the second-generation Ultra Open Earbuds has increased to nine hours from the previous seven hours.
The new Bose Sport Open Earbuds are priced at $199 and offer a secure fit, matte silicone finish, and automatic volume adjustments for active use.
Both new earbud models are available for preorder on September 19th with shipping starting October 1st.

title: The Apple Watch Series 12 is the start of a new wearable era
author: Victoria Song
content:
You wouldn’t know that the Apple Watch Series 12 is a big deal just by looking at it. It has the same design, buttons, sizes, and sensor types as generations of Apple Watches before it. But under the hood, the Series 12 builds in major changes that lay the groundwork for big ideas about the future of health and wearables.
The Apple Watch Series 12 is the start of a new wearable era
A surprisingly consequential update for the world’s most popular smartwatch.
![268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0059](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0059.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
![268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0059](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0059.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=16.666666666667%2C0%2C66.666666666667%2C100&w=2400)
These ideas — and this year’s updates — can be divided into two parts: catching up to the recent boom in AI health and leading the way in AI wearables that surface helpful information based on your entire day. When it comes to the former, Apple is catching up to the rest of the wearable space, which has eagerly embraced AI as a way to make sense of all your health data. With the latter, Apple is potentially kicking the door down on what’s been a niche, nascent, and recently problematic market. (Either way you slice it, AI is part of the equation.) Most of the ideas explored with the Series 12 aren’t novel, but they haven’t been implemented by a company with Apple’s scale or reputation.
![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0343.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=16.666666666667%2C0%2C66.666666666667%2C100&w=2400)
![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0343.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
8
Verge Score
The Good
- Faster charging
- Redesigned sensor array
- Ceramic is back
- Thoughtful privacy structure for Audio Intelligence
- Siri on the wrist is more useful
The Bad
- Thoughtful privacy may not change how laypeople feel
- Many of the new features aren’t available at launch
After a week with the Series 12, I can’t say I have a complete picture. Several of the most interesting health and AI features aren’t launching until later this year and weren’t available for review. But even without them, the revamped internals provide some meaningful upgrades. So for now, this is a look at the health features that’ll be available at launch — and a preview of the wild AI ideas to come.
New hardware
Two key hardware updates separate the Series 12 (and the Ultra 4) from previous Apple Watches. The first is the new S11 chip, which features a secure exclave for microphone data processing on top of a faster CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine. There’s also a completely redesigned health sensor array. This new array doesn’t necessarily capture new data, but it enables the watch to measure health metrics in a more frequent, accurate, and power-efficient way. The electrodes that enable the EKG feature are larger to ensure better skin contact, the photodiodes have been reconfigured to capture reflected light more efficiently, and larger, less power-hungry optical LEDs are in place to shine light into the skin.
![Close up of the Apple Watch Series 12’s new sensor array.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0208.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
Together, these hardware upgrades enable a host of new software features, including more frequent heart rate sampling, a new readiness score, and a brave new world of Audio Intelligence, which is what Apple is calling its upcoming suite of AI-powered ambient listening features.
Most notably, the redesigned sensors mean the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are now capable of truly continuous heart rate monitoring. Previously, to preserve charge, Apple Watches only sampled heart rate once every five minutes when you weren’t working out. Now, the Series 12 measures heart rate every five seconds, both at rest and during activities. Other wearable companies have been able to do this for ages, but this is a genuinely helpful update for folks who might need to monitor heart rate due to chronic illnesses.
![Siri AI is more front and center in watchOS 27.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0070.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
Apple put out a white paper comparing how accurate its continuous heart rate monitoring is to a gold-standard Polar H10 chest strap, as well as competitors like the Pixel Watch 4, Samsung Galaxy Watch 8, Oura Ring 5, and Whoop across several types of workouts and at rest. (It’s an interesting read for wearable nerds!) I’d need roughly eight arms and legs to replicate this study in a week, and alas, I’m not an octopus. However, I did wear an H10 chest strap during two runs (one steady state and one interval run), a walk, and while at rest. At all times, the Series 12 was within five beats per minute of the H10. There was a slight lag compared to the H10, but in regular use, you’re not going to notice that four-second difference.
I’ll continue testing the Series 12 and Ultra 4 against other devices and across activity types, but I’m pretty confident the Apple Watch is now in line with many other popular wearables.
The S11’s impact was also noticeable in testing. Siri AI queries are faster on the Series 12 than my Ultra 3. You still might run into latency as Siri “thinks,” but not as much. If you want more in-depth thoughts about Siri on the wrist, my opinion hasn’t changed from my watchOS 27 preview. In a nutshell, this is the most capable wrist computer Apple’s made, and adding a single pinch gesture to select items makes one-handed control the best it’s ever been.
I didn’t notice a negative impact to battery life from continuous heart rate tracking. People will gripe that the Series 12 doesn’t have multi-day battery and sticks to the Series 11’s 24-hour battery estimate. But like last year, I maintain that faster charging is a fine enough solution. In a 20-minute charging test, I went from 20 to 64 percent battery. Yes, that does mean charging daily in little spurts, but I’ve yet to have the watch die on me. I vehemently believe everyone needs to let their wrists breathe daily, and showering is the perfect time to go watchless. You’ll survive 20 to 30 minutes of no data.
Are you ready?
All this new hardware paves the way for a much more robust health tracking experience. That’s probably why, later this fall, we’re getting a new, redesigned Health app. From the demos I’ve seen, it’s going to be a dramatic change. There’ll be AI-powered insights, a longevity tab that includes a Health Age score, VO2 max assessment tests using your phone’s camera, and even the ability to order a blood panel through Quest Diagnostics for $119. The redesigned app is currently available in the latest iOS 27 developer beta, and I’ll give my early impressions on that soon. However, in this review I’m only going to talk about what’s available to everyone at launch.
The big update ready today is Apple’s take on a readiness score. Readiness scores were popularized ages ago by Fitbit, Oura, and Whoop and are meant to be a digestible gauge of how well you’ve recovered from physiological stress. In essence, how “ready” you are to work out again.
![It takes seven days to populate the readiness score, but the Vitals app now includes extra information about your overnight vitals.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0055.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
Apple assesses “readiness” through a combination of overnight, daytime, and weekly metrics like activity, sleep score, and overnight vitals encompassing resting heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and a new metric called recovery heart rate variability (HRV). You might think — wait, my Apple Watch has been able to measure HRV for years. You’d be correct. This new recovery HRV metric uses a different formula and is enabled by the fact that the watch’s updated sensor array can now take any HRV measurement much more frequently. Whereas “regular” HRV is meant to be a longitudinal look at your overall stress and cardiovascular health, Apple uses recovery HRV as a gauge of your daily, short-term strain. (And because this is enabled by the new array, it does mean readiness requires at least a Series 12 or Ultra 4.)
It takes a hot minute to generate the score — seven nights of sleep in which you get at least four hours of rest. On the eighth day, you wake up with a score from 0 to 10. A 0 to 1 means you should recover, a 2 to 4 means “pace yourself,” 5 to 7 is a benign “ready,” and anything 8 and above is a signal to “go for it.” My week of serious sleeping and accuracy testing culminated in a readiness score of 7.
![Radiant gold up top, dark bronze on the bottom.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0392.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
I’m of the opinion that people intuitively know whether they feel like working out or not. This is a feature that’s most useful for stubborn athletes who overtrain and need a reminder to not burn themselves out. I appreciate this isn’t a static score. A powerful nap or an extra hard workout could cause your readiness score to rise or fall during the day. For the Garmin nerds, I’d say it’s like a combination of Body Battery (which estimates your energy levels in real time) and traditional readiness scores. Given that wearable companies keep pumping out new metrics, I appreciate that Apple’s chosen to consolidate what could’ve been multiple data points into one.
After WWDC, I wrote that I was relieved Apple wasn’t diving full-on into AI health coaching features. I have to eat my words a teeny bit, considering Apple is clearly starting to incorporate some — though not all — of the AI health trends I’ve seen cropping up over the past two years. So far, I think Apple is carefully weighing what trends to hop on and which ones to avoid. That’s a smart long-term move. But I’m still relieved Siri AI isn’t playing a larger part just yet.
Audio Intelligence, part one
Aside from faster, more power-efficient performance, the S11 chip also enables the most surprising update to the Series 12: ambient listening. That ability is what enables Audio Intelligence, a suite of four features that essentially turn the microphone into a potentially powerful AI tool.
The two flashiest features are Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you read a short transcript on your wrist of the past 15 seconds, while the latter is a high-level summary of conversations you’ve had during the day. In this summer of public backlash against so-called pervert glasses and Flock cameras, these two features understandably stirred up a lot of concern and emotion on social media. That said, I wasn’t able to test these features because they’re not available yet. They’ll arrive later this year via a software update.
What was available to test was faster Shazam for identifying songs and sound recognition for alerting you of potentially urgent nearby noises. Both of these features require you to opt in and are not turned on by default. If you do turn on music detection, it is extremely fast. You can just pinchy pinch to bring up the Smart Stack, AI will surface the Shazam widget, and boom — there’s the song, correctly identified. (I did trip it up a teensy bit by rapidly switching between songs, but that’s not likely to happen in an organic Shazam experience.)
![The improved Shazam works in the Smart Stack. Here, Shazam is battling against ambient noise from a helicopter. Shazam did not win.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0097.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
Testing sound recognition, which is an accessibility feature for the deaf or hard of hearing, was less conclusive. It’s designed to flag on the wrist when sounds like doorbells, alarms, or sirens go off. Ironically, I haven’t had my doorbell ring this past week, but I did pull up several YouTube videos of doorbell chimes at various volumes. None triggered the feature. I think that’s a good thing. In my previous tests with other ambient listening AI wearables, they struggled to distinguish between “real” sounds and TV shows. The last thing you want is a fictional doorbell triggering an annoying, real-life alert. A blaring truck horn also didn’t trigger the feature, as it wasn’t a siren. I’ve asked Apple whether there’s specific tuning to minimize false positives, but I haven’t heard back yet.
I’ll do a deeper dive into Audio Intelligence once the whole suite of features is available. But to me, it’s clear that Apple has been taking notes about the burgeoning AI wearable space. It’s a deliberate choice to introduce these features on the Apple Watch, an already familiar and beloved device. As other tech companies deal with surveillance and harassment concerns, Apple’s published a privacy white paper and support documents to position itself as a leader trying to set a new standard. If successful with the public, it’s not a stretch to see how Apple might include these kinds of features on a pair of smart glasses or, perhaps, AirPods with camera sensors. If not, it’s no big miss. The Apple Watch is already a useful, sometimes lifesaving device without Audio Intelligence.
The most interesting, and perhaps consequential, piece of this rollout is that it comes from Apple, a wildly successful tech company with the strongest privacy reputation in Silicon Valley. If it can’t make this category of device work, that certainly doesn’t bode well for AI wearables as a whole.
Testing the waters
In many ways, this is an incomplete Series 12 review. Judging solely on what’s available today, this is a straightforward hardware upgrade that closes the gap between Apple and the standout perks of more niche rivals like Whoop and Oura.
For those pondering upgrades, Apple has laid a strong foundation with its hardware for some ambitious features down the road. I’d understand if you have qualms about Audio Intelligence and privacy, and to those folks: I’ll remind you that last year’s models are still great, probably available on sale, and don’t come with as many privacy questions.
![I’ll be back to test everything once it’s all available, but even now you can see where Apple is heading.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268738_Apple_Watch_Series_12_AKrales_0031.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
Otherwise, the Series 12 is a worthy upgrade if you’re sporting a Series 6 or earlier. Series 7 and 8 users should weigh how much they care about AI features versus their device’s current battery life, as watchOS 26 will continue to get security updates. Series 9 and later don’t need to upgrade unless, perhaps, they have a chronic illness that could benefit from the improved continuous heart rate monitoring. The excellent SE 3 remains my recommendation for smartwatch newbies who just want a basic fitness tracker. I’ll have an Ultra 4-specific review out soon, but I can already tell you that’s for folks who like big screens, better battery life, and aspire to the outdoor life.
If the Series 12 only had a new sensor array, updated Health app, and a more useful Siri on the wrist, that’d be a significant update and win on its own. But there’s a lot more here that’s going to change this product in some fundamental ways over the next few months. I have a feeling that Apple’s ambitions for the watch don’t end with health tracking.
Agree to Continue: Apple Watch Series 12
Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them, since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate.
You can only use the Apple Watch Series 12 with an iPhone. That means you’ll have already agreed to the iPhone’s terms of service and privacy agreements. Optional services, like Apple Pay, Apple Music, or Fitness Plus, will also come with their own agreements. Using the Health app also comes with its own terms and conditions. Audio Intelligence features are opt-in and are not turned on by default.
If you choose to enable cellular service, you’ll also have to agree to your carrier’s terms. I activated cellular on T-Mobile and was asked to agree to one mandatory agreement. If you add any third-party apps or integrations, you must also agree to those individual terms and privacy policies.
Specific to the Apple Watch, you must agree to the following:
Some features, like hypertension notifications, EKG, sleep apnea, or blood oxygen monitoring, may also require you to disclose your location data, as it depends on local regulatory clearances.
Final tally: One mandatory agreement plus any mandatory agreements for your iPhone. Several, several optional agreements.
summary: The Apple Watch Series 12 features familiar exterior designs while introducing major internal upgrades that lay the groundwork for a new era of AI and health features. Key updates include the new S11 chip, a redesigned health sensor array enabling continuous heart rate monitoring every five seconds, and a new daily readiness score. Although some advanced AI and health features are scheduled for release later this year, the initial hardware and software updates provide faster performance and more frequent data tracking.
key_points: The Series 12 retains the design of previous Apple Watches but introduces major internal hardware updates.
A new S11 chip and redesigned sensor array allow for truly continuous heart rate monitoring every five seconds.
A newly introduced readiness score combines overnight, daytime, and weekly metrics to gauge physical recovery and strain.
Faster charging times help maintain the 24-hour battery estimate, allowing users to charge quickly during daily routines.

title: Apple Watch Ultra 3 vs. Ultra 4 Buyer's Guide
author: Hartley Charlton
content:
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is now available for pre-order, bringing a new health sensing system, more memory, and longer battery life over its predecessor. Here's everything that's new.
![apple watch ultra 3 and ultra 4](https://images.macrumors.com/t/_lGeCbd3y3DjNKBXLd1zKMywea0=/400x0/article-new/2026/09/apple-watch-ultra-3-and-ultra-4.jpeg?lossy)
Last year, the Apple Watch Ultra 3 introduced a larger, more efficient display, satellite connectivity, 5G, and improved battery life. The Ultra 4 retains the same basic design and display, but focuses on more detailed health and fitness insights, new Audio Intelligence features, and further battery life improvements.
It launches on Friday, September 18, at the same $799 starting price as the Ultra 3. The comparison below outlines the differences between the two generations:
| Apple Watch Ultra 3 | Apple Watch Ultra 4 | 
|---|---|
| S10 chip (2024) | S11 chip (2026) | 
| 2GB RAM | 4GB RAM | 
| Electrical heart sensor | "Health Sensing System" with second-generation electrical heart sensor | 
| Third-generation optical heart sensor | Always-on optical heart sensor | 
| Background heart rate tracking | High-frequency background heart rate tracking every five seconds, 60x more frequently | 
| HRV | Recovery HRV and overall HRV, measured up to 24x more often | 
| Vitals app with heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and sleep duration | Vitals app heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, sleep duration, HRV, and a daytime vitals view | 
|  | Readiness app | 
|  | Real-time heart rate complication | 
| Step tracking | More accurate step tracking and indoor workout distance measurements | 
|  | Steps complication | 
|  | Audio Intelligence (Live Rewind, Siri Recap, Sound Recognition, and automatic music identification with Shazam) | 
| Up to 42 hours of normal use | Up to 50 hours of normal use | 
| Up to 72 hours in Low Power Mode | Up to 84 hours in Low Power Mode | 
| Up to 14 hours of outdoor workout tracking with full GPS and heart rate readings | Up to 18 hours of standard outdoor workout tracking | 
| Up to 20 hours of outdoor workout tracking in Low Power Mode with full GPS and heart rate readings | Up to 25 hours in Extended Workout mode with full GPS and heart rate readings | 
| Up to 35 hours of outdoor workout tracking in Low Power Mode with Fewer GPS and Heart Rate Readings enabled | Up to 45 hours in Max Extended Workout mode, retaining GPS readings every second | 
| 15 minutes of charging for up to 12 hours of normal use | 15 minutes of charging for up to 18 hours of normal use | 
| 5 minutes of charging for up to 8 hours of sleep tracking | 5 minutes of charging for up to 10 hours of sleep tracking | 
| Natural titanium: 61.6 grams Black titanium: 61.8 grams | Natural titanium: 63.0 grams Black titanium: 63.1 grams | 
| GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, QZSS, and BeiDou | GPS, Galileo, QZSS, and BeiDou | 
| 40% recycled content | 45% recycled content | 
| Now discontinued | From $799 | 
Is It Worth Upgrading From Ultra 3 to Ultra 4?
For the vast majority of Apple Watch Ultra 3 owners, the Ultra 4 is not worth upgrading to. The Ultra 3 already offers all of the headline display, durability, satellite connectivity, and established health features. If it comfortably lasts between your usual charging sessions and records your longest workouts, the new model is unlikely to meaningfully change how you use your watch.
The strongest reason to upgrade is if you want recovery tracking to play a larger role in your training. The Ultra 4's more frequent measurements feed into Readiness and Recovery HRV, making it easier to assess when to push harder or take a lighter day. These features are more compelling if you will regularly use them to adjust your training, rather than simply check another set of health metrics.
Battery life is a more practical reason for endurance athletes. If you currently change settings to finish long events or recharge during an extended outing, the Ultra 4 gives you a little more flexibility. For shorter daily workouts, however, the improvement mainly means less frequent charging, which is difficult to justify replacing a year-old $799 watch for.
Audio Intelligence may also justify upgrading for specific users, particularly deaf or hard of hearing users who would benefit from Sound Recognition on their wrist. Live Rewind and Siri Recap are less convincing reasons to upgrade immediately, since they arrive in beta later this year and require a compatible newer iPhone.
Should You Buy Ultra 3 or Ultra 4?
For new buyers, the Ultra 4 should be the default choice when the price difference is modest. If you plan to wear it for several years, paying a little more for the new chip, more memory, better battery life, and health tracking enhancements is easier to justify than replacing an Ultra 3 you already own.
The Ultra 3 becomes the better value when it is heavily discounted. If you mainly want a "rugged"-style Apple Watch with a large screen, satellite connectivity, and enough battery life for everyday use and regular workouts, it delivers much of the same experience. Buyers interested in Readiness and recovery insights, or who regularly record very long activities, have a stronger reason to pay more for the Apple Watch Ultra 4.
For used or refurbished Ultra 3 models, factor battery condition and warranty coverage into the saving. A cheaper watch with a degraded battery is less appealing if endurance is your main reason for buying an Ultra.
summary: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 launches on September 18 starting at $799, offering a new health sensing system, double the memory, Audio Intelligence features, and extended battery life compared to the Ultra 3. While the new model is recommended for new buyers and endurance athletes seeking better battery and recovery tracking, the article suggests it is not a necessary upgrade for current Ultra 3 owners.
key_points: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 retains the basic design and $799 starting price of the Ultra 3 while adding an S11 chip, 4GB of RAM, and new Audio Intelligence features.
Health updates include a new Health Sensing System, more frequent heart rate and HRV tracking, a Readiness app, and more accurate step and workout distance measurements.
Battery life is improved, offering up to 50 hours of normal use and up to 84 hours in Low Power Mode.

For current Ultra 3 owners, upgrading is generally not recommended unless they specifically want advanced recovery tracking, better battery flexibility for endurance events, or Sound Recognition features.
New buyers should choose the Ultra 4 by default for longevity, while the Ultra 3 remains a good value option if heavily discounted.

title: I’ve tried the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, here’s my full review
author: Andrew Griffin
content:
The Pro version of the iPhone is not used to being upstaged. It is usually the headlining star of Apple’s entire product line, packed with the very latest and best technology the company has. This year, however, that’s not the case: the iPhone 18 Pro arrives alongside the iPhone Duo – and it’s the folding phone that has taken much of the limelight.
This year, the iPhone 18 Pro also arrives without an iPhone 18, further complicating the line-up. For now, Apple is just selling the still-brilliant iPhone 17, though rumours suggest that an updated version of the base model will arrive in the spring. Last year, the choice was relatively simple: if you wanted the latest and greatest iPhone, get the Pro, but if it is a little too expensive then you could get the base version and not miss out on much.
Nonetheless, the iPhone 18 Pro is still packed with a host of changes that make it a meaningful upgrade from last year’s Pro model, and it remains the device that most people will still be looking to buy this year. There are few changes on the outside, beyond a new colour and a slightly altered screen, but some dramatic improvements on the inside. But is it enough to keep the iPhone 18 Pro on top of the phone market? Here’s my full review after testing the iPhone 18 Pro for a week.
Read more: My first impressions of the iPhone Duo
![iPhone 18 Pro](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/16/10/14/IMG_6016dmuGY9.png?quality=75&width=703&crop=3%3A2%2Csmart&trim=83%2C0%2C83%2C0&auto=webp)
- Display Pro: 6.3in OLED, 120Hz, 2,622 x 1,206 pixels, 460ppi or Pro max: 6.9in OLED, 120Hz, 2,868 x 1,320 pixels, 460ppi
- CPU Apple A20 Pro
- Storage 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB
- Size Pro: 150mm x 71.9mm x 8.75mm or Pro Max: 163.4mm x 78mm x 8.75mm
- Main camera 48MP (with new variable aperture)
- Ultra Wide camera 48MP
- Telephoto camera 48MP
- Selfie camera 18MP
- Why we love it 
  - Beautiful, reliable and sturdy design
 
  - Even better camera system
 
  - Battery and performance improvements mean you never have to worry
- Take note 
  - Already pricey – and now even more so
 
  - Could be upstaged by folding iPhone Duo
iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max: Design and display
The most obvious change in this year’s iPhone design is the addition of a new colour. It’s burgundy, which is the company’s hero colour this year – you can get a whole host of accessories from Apple Watch bands to cross-body straps in it, and new chief executive John Ternus even wore a burgundy shirt during the introduction.
![The iPhone 18 Pro's new burgundy colour is not quite as eye-catching as last year's 'Cosmic Orange' – but is rich and subtle (Andrew Griffin/The Independent)](<https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/16/11/25/IMG_6022C4Ehjr.png?quality=75&width=608&auto=webp 608w>)
It’s a long way from the “cosmic orange” that served the same purpose last year: unlike that colour, which announced itself loudly and shouted that you had the new Pro, this new colour is deep, rich and subtle. It looks expensive (which it is; the iPhone Pro was already pricey and has had a £100 upgrade, as discussed below). If that doesn’t do it for you then there are actually plenty of other new colours, too: a new “glacier” one that is a similarly subtle silvery-blue, a proper black returns to the line-up, and then there is the classic silver.
Another small tweak to the colours means that the matte glass panel that is on the back of the phone – to allow wireless charging to pass through its otherwise aluminium body – is now better colour-matched to the rest of the phone. This makes the design look a little more cohesive, though the slight mismatch on last year’s models made for an interesting two-tone effect, depending on how the light hit it.
The only other change that’s visible from the outside is a smaller version of the Dynamic Island cutout that sits near the top of the display, and contains sensors for the camera and Face ID unlock technology. It has become smaller because Apple has moved some of the Face ID tech under the display, to the top left, where information including the network is shown. It’s almost entirely imperceptible, apart from at some angles, and it doesn’t really matter when you do see it because it sits in a part of the screen that doesn’t often show particularly important information.
The smaller notch means that the phone can now show three of the “live activities” that spring out from that Dynamic Island, displaying information such as your music or directions as you use the rest of your phone. The things that can trigger live activities are relatively rare though, for instance you’d have to be listening to music, getting directions and following sports scores all at once – but it’s neat to have the option.
Beyond those small tweaks, the design and display of the iPhone 18 Pro are unchanged from last year’s models. In fact, they’re so similar that you can happily put an iPhone 17 Pro into an iPhone 18 Pro case. Last year’s update brought a whole new and very welcome look to the Pro phones, so it was always unlikely that Apple would make any big changes, especially given everything else it has going on this year.
That means, however, that with the iPhone 18 Pro you get access to all of the great upgrades that have come in recent years. The display is beautiful: bright even on a sunny day, crisp enough that you almost forget it is there, smooth in a way that’s noticeable when you go back to a model that doesn’t have Apple’s ProMotion technology. And the build of the iPhone 18 Pro is robust. The materials and case design are the same as the iPhone 17 Pro, which has survived me dropping it an embarrassing number of times over the last year. The screen has stayed largely unblemished and the sturdy aluminium design means that any dings actually give it a kind of nice, outdoorsy patina, and there's no reason to think the new 18 Pro won't be the same.
As with last year, the only difference between the Pro and Pro Max are their size; they have all the same features otherwise. With the Max, you just get a larger display (and, of course, a larger phone in your pocket), as well as slightly more battery life thanks to that extra space. The choice really comes down to whether you want that bigger display and the bigger phone, as well as the slightly larger price tag (it starts from £1,299 for 256GB).
iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max: Cameras
Perhaps the most impressive – and technically bewildering – feature of the new camera is its new variable aperture setting on the main camera. That means that the phone’s lens can work like one on a bigger, SLR camera: opening or closing the hole in front of the lens, to decide how much light is allowed through.
Because of the size constraints, Apple had to do this in an astonishingly impressive, if entirely invisible, way. To open and close the aperture, the phone moves little pieces of material – thinner than a human hair – around the lens. But you aren’t aware of that happening, and Apple has stressed that the technology went through intense testing to ensure that it remains robust and not likely to break despite its delicacy.
The most obvious way that this matters is that the phone can open up the aperture so that it allows more light through, for better performance in dark conditions. Apple says that this gives about 50 per cent better low-light performance – and while it is hard to judge exactly what that means in practice, photos taken in the dark are crisper, brighter and much less likely to be smudged by motion blur.
The aperture changes also mean mean that you can dig in and change them if you want. Apple offers the option to change the aperture all the way up from its biggest 1.48 to 4 – letting the phone capture more detail from across the scene, such as the background, as well as allowing for flashy new effects like the “starburst” that happens on bright parts of the scene.
To get the most out of the new phone’s cameras, you can dig into the camera’s settings, and iOS 27 brings detailed controls for changes such as shutter speed and white balance, as well as that aperture. The new phone also has an updated version of Apple’s photographic styles, which let you fiddle with grain and skin tone, as well as allowing for a film-like look.
Those controls are convenient and instinctual – but they also disappear if you don’t want them, and you wouldn’t even need to know they are there. The iPhone 18 Pro’s camera now offers expansive customisation but also enough smarts that you can just point and click, and the phone will adjust everything including the new aperture to make sure you are getting the best photo it can take.
It means that the camera in the Pro is the best of Apple’s design: finely customisable if you want it, but stunningly simple when you don’t. And the photos that it produces are representative of that. For pointing and shooting, especially in low light, the new Pro models are so capable that you hardly have to think about it until you look back on a picture and marvel at just how crisp and detailed it looks. But if you do want to think about it, then you can, and the phone is capable of shooting spectacular, professional-level photos and videos if you want to use it that way.
iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max: Performance
Some of the biggest improvements in this year’s phone are entirely invisible. Apple has made a whole host of new performance improvements – most notably its new A20 Pro chip, and a new cooling system – that mean that the phone should run more quickly, stably and cooler.
The chip is up to 50 per cent faster than the previous model, according to Apple’s own claims. Those are proved by our testing in benchmarks, which take the phone through a representative if slightly artificial set of tasks to see how it can handle them. It has better AI capabilities as well as a whole range of other improvements that mean that the phone can run incredibly fast, much faster than previous models – which were already best-in-class.
The difference is harder to test in practice, especially over such a short period. But the phone is snappy in daily use, and impressively capable at handling complex tasks such as running complex AI models. Using the new Siri AI feature even on the iPhone 17 Pro could sometimes mean waiting for a response; with the iPhone 18 Pro, that is almost entirely gone.
The truth is that the iPhone 18 Pro’s increased power is most notable in what you don’t see. Whatever you throw at the phone, it does, and you never see it slow or have any kind of trouble. It means that the processor can do what you ask of it and then power down again, which is an important part of the battery improvements outlined below. Few people are likely to push the A20 Pro to its very limits – in truth, iPhones have been more than capable of the daily work of texting, using social media and taking photos for years – but you don’t actually need to be pushing at its boundaries to experience the benefits.
The more obvious difference in performance is the new cooling system. Last year, Apple introduced a vapour chamber to the Pro models, which uses water inside the phone to move heat around and let it dissipate more quickly. This year, that vapour chamber is much bigger and the phone’s internals have been moved around to make better use of it – which Apple says means up to 40 per cent better sustained performance, useful when doing long, intense work such as AI models or gaming.
That change is similarly hard to test over such a short period. But, just like the new chip, it is notable in part by what you don’t notice: the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max simply refuse to get hot, even while charging, in hot weather, and doing intense tasks. As well as the boost to high-end performance, it means that you are much less likely to run into those less glamorous problems that come with a hot phone, when the display brightness tunes itself down, it starts to run slow, and sometimes even refuses to work at all.
iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max: Battery life
Apple has made dramatic strides with its battery life in recent years, and this year’s models continue that further. Apple says that the iPhone 18 Pro Max will work for 29 hours of typical use, and up to 43 hours of video playback, a six-hour increase. The smaller Pro model has the same (remarkably long-lasting) battery life as last year’s bigger Max model.
This is hard to test in such a short period: new iPhones get busy downloading, indexing and much more besides as soon as you take them out of the box. That’s even more notable than usual this year – since the phones also have access to Siri AI, which makes the voice assistant vastly more useful but requires a complex process at launch to learn all the information it needs about you to work. Both of these things mostly happen only when the phone is charging, helpfully.
But in the first week, Apple’s claims that both sizes of the iPhone 18 Pro will comfortably last you through the day, certainly seem to stack up. While the precise numbers of the improvement still need more testing, they come together to mean something important and clearly true: you won’t need to worry about charging this phone through the day.
When you do need to charge it, that’s improved too. The phone has faster wired charging that means that you can get the iPhone 18 Pro up to 50 per cent charge in 15 minutes, with the right plug, so it’s quick and simple to top up.
iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max pricing
Pricing for the Pro starts at £1,199 in the UK, and £1,299 for the Max. You can go all the way up to £2,499 for the biggest options of display and storage.
That is at least a £100 increase from last year’s Pro phones, and the most expensive model is £500 more than the equivalent last year. But the same price increase has gone into effect across the line-up, including for instance for last year’s cheaper iPhone 17 and 17e. Apple didn’t explicitly say why, but the hike comes after it pushed up the prices of devices across its line-up, in response to a chip crisis that has made parts more expensive.
It means that this year’s Pro line-up is undeniably pricey, though not of course as pricey as the iPhone Duo that starts at £1,999 and can be upgraded to much more than that. But it also means that the choice is largely the same: all of the devices are more expensive, so represent similar value for money, relatively.
summary: The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max bring meaningful internal upgrades including the A20 Pro chip, a new cooling system, and an advanced main camera with a variable aperture, while maintaining a familiar exterior design with a new burgundy color option. Despite facing competition for attention from Apple's new folding phone, the iPhone 18 Pro continues to deliver top-tier performance, enhanced low-light photography, and reliable battery life. However, these new models also come with a price increase.
key_points: Features a new burgundy color option and a slightly smaller Dynamic Island cutout enabled by moving parts of the Face ID technology under the display.
Introduces a new variable aperture on the 48MP main camera utilizing microscopic moving parts for about 50 percent better low-light performance.
Powered by the new A20 Pro chip and a larger vapour chamber cooling system, delivering faster performance and preventing the phone from overheating.
The Pro and Pro Max models are functionally identical except for their physical size, larger display, and increased battery life on the Max version.
The iPhone 18 Pro has seen a £100 price increase compared to previous iterations.

title: macOS 27.2 beta 1 now available to developers, here’s what’s new - 9to5Mac
author: Marcus Mendes
content:
![](https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/09/macOS-27.2-b1.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1600) 
Now that macOS 27 Golden Gate is officially out, Apple is moving on to its next beta cycle, straight to macOS 27.2 beta 1. Here are the details.
macOS 27.2 beta 1 now available
After releasing macOS 27 Golden Gate earlier this week, Apple is now rolling out the first developer beta of macOS 27.2, skipping over the 27.1 betas.
As for what to expect from this release, during its “Surprise and Shine” event earlier this month, Apple said that the new Siri AI, which launched in English, would expand to five more languages in October, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. This means developers might find these languages in this first beta.
Additionally, Apple has yet to confirm a new rollout date for two features it announced during WWDC but didn’t make it to the first macOS 27 release: an agentic feature in Passwords that will automatically change leaked passwords, and suggestions in Messages conversations.
We are digging through the code to check whether these made it to macOS 27.2 beta 1 and will report back with what we find.
macOS 27.2 beta 1 release build is 26B5086k.
Installing macOS 27.2 beta 1
![](https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/09/macos27.2-b1.jpg?quality=82&strip=all)
Here’s how to install the first macOS 27.2 beta 1:
- Back up your Mac
- Open System Settings
- Go to General ⇾ Software Update
- Click the ‘i’ icon next to Beta Updates
- From the dropdown menu in the top-right, select the macOS Developer Golden Gate Beta
- Hit ‘Done’
Did you spot anything new in today’s macOS 27.2 Golden Gate beta 1? Let us know in the comments.
Worth checking out on Amazon

![Add 9to5Mac as a preferred source on Google](https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/themes/ninetofive/dist/images/google-preferred-source-badge-light.png)

![](https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/09/09-10-iPhone-18-Pro-Ghost-Banner.png)
summary: Apple has released the first developer beta of macOS 27.2, skipping the 27.1 beta cycle shortly after rolling out macOS 27 Golden Gate. The new beta build is 26B5086k and can be installed via System Settings under Software Update. Developers are currently investigating the code to see if it includes expanded Siri AI languages or previously delayed WWDC features.
key_points: Apple released macOS 27.2 beta 1 to developers with build number 26B5086k.
The release skips the macOS 27.1 beta cycle following the rollout of macOS 27 Golden Gate.
The update may include expanded Siri AI support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.
Developers are checking whether delayed WWDC features like automatic leaked password changes and Messages suggestions are present.

title: With iOS 27, Apple Is Laying the Groundwork to Paywall Your iPhone
author: Gabriel Zamora
content:
![](https://sm.pcmag.com/t/pcmag_uk/opinion/w/with-ios-2/with-ios-27-apple-is-laying-the-groundwork-to-paywall-your-i_us2z.1920.jpg) (Credit: Eric Zeman)
Historically, the annual iOS rollout acts as the great equalizer: Whether you're holding a brand-new flagship or a three-year-old device, updating your software feels like a free upgrade. But look closely at the iPhone over the last few years, and you'll see fault lines beginning to form.
Ever since Apple entered the relentless silicon arms race on phones, it has widened the gap between its standard processors and its ultra-premium chips. Newer hardware generations leave previous ones in the dust. We used to upgrade our phones for better cameras and speed. Lately, though, we're upgrading just to keep our software from feeling second-class.
With iOS 27, that slow burn has reached a boiling point. Apple’s latest operating system introduces a brutal new economic division. It splits iPhone owners into a three-tier caste system based on hardware age, RAM capacity, and eventually, the thickness of their wallets.
Siri AI Is Genius, Exclusionary Tech
I experienced this division firsthand. I downloaded the iOS 27 update, unlocked my phone, and immediately swiped through my Home Screen looking for the marquee feature. Where was the new standalone Siri AI app? Why did my device look exactly the same? As it turns out, I had to open my settings, scroll down, and manually register for a waitlist just to get in line for my phone's new brain.
Once I got past the gate, I put the new Siri AI to the test. I wanted to push its limits, so I initiated a complex brainstorming session about a steam-powered airship concept. To my genuine surprise, Siri was incredible: The fluid, natural back-and-forth resembled an advanced generative AI chatbot workspace. It is, without a doubt, a fantastic and genuinely useful tool to have built into a smartphone.
But a much larger, uglier truth quickly overshadowed my optimism: If you don't belong to the right iPhone caste, you are locked out. If you're on an iPhone 15 or older, you don't get this technology. My own iPhone 15 Pro barely made the cut, and by next year, I can't be sure it still will.
![](https://sm.pcmag.com/pcmag_uk/photo/s/siri-ai-in/siri-ai-in-action_1uwn.jpg) (Credit: Apple/PCMag)
Inside Apple's Uncomfortable iPhone Caste System
To understand the new three-tier iPhone ecosystem is to understand a structure of deliberate digital segregation. Apple has fractured its user base along lines of hardware age, spending power, and how quickly you adopt new tech. It's no longer about owning an iPhone; it's about which class of iPhone you can afford to stay in.
At the bottom of this new hierarchy are the grandfathered iPhones. Apple boasts that iOS 27 supports legacy devices all the way back to the iPhone 11. But if you own a standard iPhone 15 or older, you get optimizations, not new features. Look past the faster app launches, and you'll realize your phone isn’t getting smarter. You are locked out of the Siri AI workspace.
The middle tier would be any more recent iPhone, such as the 15 Pro, the base iPhone 16 or 17, and so on. But the fragmentation doesn't stop at artificial intelligence. iOS 27 introduces a variant of the OS that's strictly designed to reward the highest spenders. At the apex of this hierarchy, in the highest tier, is the newly unveiled iPhone Duo class.
For years, Apple power users have practically begged for basic productivity features, such as the ability to run two applications simultaneously. Apple repeatedly restricted the feature, treating split-screen multitasking as a sacred boundary reserved only for the iPad or a desktop.
But the adaptive version of iOS 27 on the iPhone Duo shatters that philosophy. Unfold the Duo’s massive canvas, and iOS 27 unlocks native, side-by-side app multitasking with unique app-pairing engines. By gating a baseline software feature like split-screen multitasking behind an eye-watering price tag, Apple is sending a clear message: Basic digital efficiency is no longer an inherent part of the smartphone experience. Instead, it’s an upmarket luxury.
Apple Intelligence Is a Trojan Horse
Even if you hold an iPhone with enough RAM to clear the AI gateway and join the middle tier, such as the brand-new iPhone 18 Pro Max, you're only safe for now. Though Apple doesn't consider your device obsolete just yet, the powerful AI features you enjoy with iOS 27 may well be subject to future restrictions. Tucked away in the official footnotes of Apple's launch documentation is a philosophical shift: Server-side features like Siri AI and Image Playground are subject to daily usage limits.
![](https://sm.pcmag.com/pcmag_uk/photo/t/the-new-si/the-new-siri-app-lets-you-revisit-past-conversations-or-star_e5wh.jpg) (Credit: Apple)
Apple is giving users a temporary, free taste of a truly intelligent assistant right now to hook them into the workflow. But the billing tollbooth is already being built. Apple's own terms explicitly state that "increased access to such features will be available for a fee" in the future.
By the time the next software cycle hits, Apple will flip the switch and demand a paid subscription for extended access to your phone’s own brain. If you want to keep using the excellent conversational assistant that just helped you map out a steampunk airship, you’ll have to pay a recurring fee or buy into the elite hardware tier.
Silicon Valley has spent years trying to turn physical hardware into a recurring software subscription. With iOS 27, Apple is finally doing it, and the iPhone may never be the same.
summary: Apple's iOS 27 creates a new three-tier ecosystem that divides iPhone users based on hardware age, RAM capacity, and spending power. Advanced features like the new Siri AI workspace and split-screen multitasking are restricted to newer, higher-end devices or locked behind exclusive hardware classes like the iPhone Duo. Additionally, Apple's documentation indicates that server-side AI features will eventually be subjected to daily usage limits and future paid subscriptions.
key_points: iOS 27 introduces a three-tier caste system that separates iPhone users based on hardware capabilities and spending power.
Owners of the iPhone 15 and older are largely locked out of the new standalone Siri AI workspace.
Split-screen multitasking is gated behind the expensive, newly unveiled iPhone Duo class.
Apple's launch documentation hints that server-side AI features will eventually require a fee or subscription for extended access.

title: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max Review: Fastest phones ever, variable aperture camera soars
author: Mark Spoonauer
content:
Tom's Guide Verdict
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max raise the bar for performance in a phone with the new A20 Pro chip. You also get a versatile new variable aperture camera that takes brighter images and gives you more creative control. The battery life from both devices is awesome, too, and you get the fastest charging yet from an iPhone. You have to pay $100 more for both Pro phones, and they’re heavier than their predecessors, but overall these are easily the best phones money can buy.
Pros
- +Fastest chip in a phone
- +Variable aperture camera
- +New Pro controls
- +Super long battery life
- +Smarter Siri AI
- +Faster charging
Cons
- -$100 price hike
- -Heavier designs
Why you can trust Tom's Guide
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max don’t have a ‘wow’ feature to flex to your friends like the iPhone Duo. Yet beneath the familiar design is a pretty big leap forward for two areas people really care about: cameras and performance.
With a new variable aperture main camera, the iPhone 18 Pro lets in more light and gives you more creative freedom than ever before with new Pro controls. And the A20 Pro chip — the first 2nm chip in a phone — delivers record-breaking speed that surpasses all Android flagships. Based on our testing, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max battery life is stellar, too. And with the new Siri AI on board these Pro phones are much more capable personal assistants.
![iPhone 18 Pro Performance & Battery TESTED: The A20 Pro Is Ridiculous! - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/QJVNbFMd-zQ/maxresdefault.jpg) 
The bad news? The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are noticeably heavier than their predecessors, and the prices are $100 higher for both models. But if you’ve been putting off that upgrade for a while, you'll find that both of these Pros are the best phones you can buy.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Specs
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | iPhone 18 Pro | iPhone 18 Pro Max | 
| Price | From $1,199 | From $1,299 | 
| Main Display | 6.3-inch Super Retina XDR display (2,622 x 1,206) | 6.9-inch Super Retina XDR display (2,868 x 1,320) | 
| Processor | A20 Pro | A20 Pro | 
| Storage | 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB | 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB | 
| RAM | 12GB | 12GB | 
| Front Camera | 18MP Center Stage camera (f/1.9) | 18MP Center Stage camera (f/1.9) | 
| Rear Cameras | 48MP main with variable aperture (f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, f/4), 48MP ultrawide (f/2.2), 48MP telephoto w/4x optical zoom (f/2.8) | 48MP main with variable aperture (f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, f/4), 48MP ultrawide (f/2.2), 48MP telephoto w/4x optical zoom (f/2.8) | 
| Battery Life Video Playback | Up to 36 hours | Up to 45 hours | 
| Charging | 60W, 35W wireless | 60W, 35W wireless | 
| Size | 5.91 x 2.83 x 0.34 inches (150.0 x 71.9 x 8.75 mm) | 6.43 x 3.07 x 0.34 inches (163.4 x 78.0 x 8.75 mm) | 
| Weight | 7.44 ounces (211 grams) | 8.78 ounces (249 grams) | 
| IP Rating | IP68 | IP68 | 
| Colors | Black, Silver, Glacier, Burgundy | Black, Silver, Glacier, Burgundy | 
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max Performance: Fastest phones ever
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/VEw4CiZWCodwwRopC8qNoK.jpg) 
The A20 Pro chip isn’t just the world’s first 2nm chip inside a smartphone; it’s the fastest one we’ve ever tested, blowing away the Android competition.
You get a new CPU with two super cores that are up to 20% faster and four efficiency cores, a 7-core GPU that’s up to 40 percent faster (up from 6 cores) and a new dual 16-core Neural Engine for better AI performance. Plus, there’s a wider memory interface that provides up to 50% more internal bandwidth.
It’s all wrapped up in a new package design that seats the memory next to the SoC instead of on top, which results in better heat dissipation. In fact, the vapor chamber itself has 3x the surface area to deliver better sustained performance (aka, less overheating). So how about the results? They’re pretty staggering.
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Geekbench 6 (single/multi-core) | Geekbench 7 | 3DMark Solar Bay Unlimited | Geekbench AI 1.7 | 
| iPhone 18 Pro | 4,735 / 12,800 | 4,022 / 11,543 | 61.93 fps / 16,288 | 69245 (Quantitized Core ML/Neural Engine) | 
| iPhone 18 Pro Max | 4,741 / 12,789 | 4,025 / 11,525 | 67.9 fps/17,850 | 71974 | 
| Galaxy S26 Ultra | 3,785 / 11,563 | 3,149 / 10,612 | 49.37 fps / 12,984 | 83047 (TensorFlow Lite QNN) | 
| iPhone 17 Pro | 3,834/ 9,988 | 3,138 / 8,692 | 46.4 fps / 12,208 | 49,050 | 
| iPhone 17 Pro Max | 3,871 / 9,968 | 3,285 / 8,999 | 46.6 fps / 12,260 | 48549 | 
On Geekbench 6, which measures overall performance, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max scored in the 4,700 range in the single core portion. That’s about 25% higher than the iPhone 17 Pro series and also 25% faster than the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy chip.
Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.
In terms of multi-core performance, the A20 Pro once again excelled, offering a 28% boost versus the iPhone 17 Pros. And we’re talking about a 10% advantage over the Galaxy S26 Ultra here.
We also ran the newer Geekbench 7, which has a multi-core benchmark that’s designed to be more real-world and uses more challenging data sets. The iPhone 18 Pro delivered similar performance gains.
The graphics leap is even more impressive from the A20 Pro. On the 3DMark Solar Bay Unlimited test, the iPhone 18 Pro turned in a frame rate of 62 fps, which is 33% faster than the 17 Pro. And the iPhone 18 Pro Max scored an even higher 67.9 fps, which is 45% faster than the 17 Pro Max.
The Galaxy S26 Ultra just couldn’t keep up, as the regular iPhone 18 Pro was 25% faster and the iPhone 18 Pro Max was 37% higher.
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/36uFQPaegizL2WM4jr82pH.jpg) 
When playing the game Ungodly, the gameplay remained fluid even while I was slicing through three enemies at once with my sword. And the animations looked just as crisp as console gameplay when I switched characters and rained down fire attacks on my enemies.
So how about Apple’s sustained performance claims? Thanks to the larger vapor chamber and design of the A20 Pro chip, Apple promises up to a 40% improvement. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max did indeed impress when we ran the 3DMark Wild Life Extreme Stress Test, which loops through a graphics test 20 times in a row.
| Sustained Performance |  | 
|---|---|
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | 3DMark Wild Life Extreme Stress Test Stability Score | 
| iPhone 18 Pro | 62.8% | 
| iPhone 18 Pro Max | 79.4% | 
| Galaxy S26 Ultra | 53.9% | 
| iPhone 17 Pro | 61.1% | 
| iPhone 17 Pro Max | 65.2% | 
The iPhone 18 Pro Max turned in a stability score of 79.4%, which is 25% better than the iPhone 17 Pro Max. That’s also over 47% better than the Galaxy S26 Ultra. However, we saw only a minor 1.7% gain between the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro.
Last but not least we tested AI performance using the Geekbench AI test. The iPhone 18 Pro turned in a Neural Engine score of 69,245 and the iPhone 18 Pro Max a much higher 71,974. That’s a boost of 41 to 48%, which means on-device AI tasks should run faster.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Battery life and charging
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/sQDrYHT2bXbjRsmmPzXQaJ.jpg) 
Thanks to the efficiency of the A20 Pro chip and bigger batteries, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is rated to have the longest battery life ever of any iPhone. And the iPhone 18 Pro is rated for the endurance of last year’s iPhone 17 Pro Max, which made our best phone battery life list last year.
The good news is that both the iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone 18 Pro last longer than their 17 Pro counterparts. But we didn’t see a huge leap in endurance.
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Hrs:Mins | 
| iPhone 18 Pro Max | 18:27 | 
| iPhone 18 Pro | 16:17 | 
| iPhone 17 Pro Max | 17:54 | 
| iPhone 17 Pro | 15:21 | 
| Galaxy S26 Ultra | 16:40 | 
| OnePlus 15 | 25:13 | 
On the Tom’s Guide battery test, which involves continuous web surfing over 5G on 150 nits of screen brightness, the iPhone 18 Pro Max lasted 18 hours and 41 minutes on its longest run and averaged 18:27. The iPhone 17 Pro Max lasted 17:54.
The iPhone 18 Pro lasted an average of 16:17 on our test, which is nearly an hour longer than the iPhone 17 Pro (15:21).
By comparison, the Galaxy S26 Ultra averaged 16:40 with the display mode set to standard and 16:10 in adaptive mode. So the iPhone 18 Pro Max lasts about 2 hours longer on a charge.
The OnePlus 15 is still the champ with its silicon carbon battery at 25 hours and 13 minutes. It will be interesting to see what happens when (or if) Apple embraces this technology for itself.
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max both support 60W charging for the first time, and Apple promises a 30% charge in just 15 minutes. The iPhone 18 Pro hit 53% in 15 minutes and 80% in 30 minutes, but the iPhone 18 Pro Max was a bit behind with 44% and 77%, respectively.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max Cameras: What variable aperture can do
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/b2pgpnQKaxpBNTMcJ7oQjK.jpg) 
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have a first for iPhones, even though the Samsung Galaxy S9 tried it years ago. I’m talking about a variable aperture main camera. There’s six tiny blades inside the wide lens that can expand or contract depending on the conditions.
For example, if you’re taking a portrait, the aperture might open up to f/1.48 to let in more light. And if you want more detail throughout the shot, the iPhone 18 Pro Max might stop down to f/4.0. This gives you more depth of field.
The iPhone 18 Pro’s camera can do this all automatically, but there’s new Pro controls on board that lets you set the exact aperture with four options.
![iPhone 18 Pro Max aperture f/4.0](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/SGfp5XiUJsGDo2kUU43cob-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max aperture f/1.8](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/QVLjmGvb9JGFx8FxZ8ByVb-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max aperture f/4.0](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/SGfp5XiUJsGDo2kUU43cob-1280-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max aperture f/1.8](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/QVLjmGvb9JGFx8FxZ8ByVb-1280-80.jpg) 
In the above portrait, you can see that the menu in the background is blurred out at f/1.48, but it's clear when I set it to f/4.
 ![photo of flowers in Bryant Park in front of stage](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/2CVrvHDZ35dFvy9xEo78rX.jpg) 
When I captured a photo of begonias in Bryant Park, I selected f/1.48 to blur the background and f/4.0 to bring detail to the stage across the park and buildings.
The wider aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max also enables the phones to let in significantly more light overall, which means better low-light images.
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/XThNBx9PUHMu43tZ7KXvib-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/NYycWYrSVQm4kL4CMRWqVb-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/PS6QSXpornvyno7hLNKeCa-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/XThNBx9PUHMu43tZ7KXvib-1280-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/NYycWYrSVQm4kL4CMRWqVb-1280-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/PS6QSXpornvyno7hLNKeCa-1280-80.jpg) 
Take this American flag photo captured in near darkness. You can make out more detail in the flag pole and the brick in the iPhone 18 Pro image. The Galaxy S26 Ultra shot is downright blurry.
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/9wpEQa3DwhwP4D3HH5A87b-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/M7g2su3MgqDhzvuQbZbSVb-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/9wpEQa3DwhwP4D3HH5A87b-1280-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/M7g2su3MgqDhzvuQbZbSVb-1280-80.jpg) 
Indoors I’d give a slight edge to the iPhone 18 Pro with this shot of Halloween decorations. The dots of light reflecting off the transparent orb look sharper through the iPhone. But the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s photo has more saturated colors inside the ball and in the fabric.
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/UaBpbCqvrKtnvGjwpz92Qc-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/f5pR7L5C9dFRbT23GnhJLc-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/eSTAqV88gqTcQTtsx2PHNc-1200-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/UaBpbCqvrKtnvGjwpz92Qc-1280-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/f5pR7L5C9dFRbT23GnhJLc-1280-80.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/eSTAqV88gqTcQTtsx2PHNc-1280-80.jpg) 
As you can see in the gallery above, the iPhone 18 Pro takes a better looking shot of produce (the red peppers don’t look right through the Samsung).
When it comes to zoom power, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max hold their own with a 4x telephoto lens and 8x optical quality zoom. The iPhone is neck and neck with Samsung with this 10x zoom shot of a pumpkin.
However, at 40x the iPhone really struggles versus the S26 Ultra. Check out the sign above. I'm sure the Galaxy is doing some AI processing, but the test is definitely sharper in its photo.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Video
My favorite video feature when testing the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max is the ability to add Cinematic mode to your clips after the fact. You no longer have to select the mode before you start shooting.
![iPhone 18 Pro: Cinematic Mode on - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/t7LuoywmKb0/maxresdefault.jpg) 
![iPhone 18 Pro: Cinematic Mode off - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/-XgH2ozgkDU/maxresdefault.jpg) 
I had someone capture a video of me walking down a park trail. Afterwards, I toggled the Cinematic mode feature in editing right at the top of the screen. Sure enough, the iPhone 18 Pro added an artful blur to the footage.
Other new features include 4K Timelapse in Dolby Vision HDR, higher-quality low-light video in 1080p resolution and Pro controls for video, such as shutter speed.
![iPhone 18 Pro: Daylight (4K, 30 fps, HDR) - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/wGhxKbJTPPc/maxresdefault.jpg) 
To test out the iPhone 18 Pro’s video capabilities I shot this koi pond with a fountain using the new iPhone and Galaxy S26 Ultra at 4K at 30 fps with HDR turned on. I prefer the way the iPhone 18 Pro renders the details in the rocks and its smoother zooming motion; the S26 Ultra takes a second to regain focus. However, the S26 Ultra’s superior zoom shines when I get really close on the fountain wall.
![Galaxy S26 Ultra: Daylight (4K, 30 fps, HDR) - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/WbWvPo_lHrs/maxresdefault.jpg) 
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Siri AI and Apple Intelligence
 ![Siri AI on an iPhone 18 Pro](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/UHFLgbZkizWAuzbea6ATRH.jpg) 
I’m not going to say that Siri AI is smarter than Gemini or ChatGPT yet, but it’s come a long way with iOS 27, and is now a lot more helpful. That’s because Siri now better understands your personal context, and it can let you do multiple things with a single voice prompt.
For example, I asked Siri to look up reviews for a hotel I was thinking of staying at with my brother for a road trip and send them via text in the same prompt. The results seemed okay but didn’t have as much detail as I’d like. So I tried again, asking for best dishes.
I can also control three different apps with the same prompt, such as setting a reminder, starting a timer and looking up photos and adding them to a Note. The new Siri AI is smarter and more powerful, but sometimes it started doing the first thing I asked before I got to the second request, interrupting the flow.
Visual Intelligence also gets an upgrade with iOS 27 and the iPhone 18 Pros. For example, I pointed the iPhone 18 Pro Max at a flyer with a bunch of dates on it, and it automatically recognized the dates and asked if I wanted to add them to my calendar. I especially like that there’s a dedicated Siri mode in the camera app so you don’t have to go to a separate app.
However, Siri AI is not quite as robust as Gemini or ChatGPT Voice. You can’t have a live back-and-forth conversation about what’s live in your camera view. This comes in quite handy for troubleshooting.
Other helpful Apple Intelligence features include contextually relevant cards that pop up when you’re texting. For example, you might get a prompt to add something to your calendar or reminders with a little icon.
Some of the coolest Apple Intelligence upgrades live in the camera app. For example, with Reframe you can change the angle of your photo after the fact. I did this with a photo of my daughter and the iPhone 18 Pro Max basically guessed what the background was of the pier and filled it in.
In addition, you can extend the background of your photos via Apple Intelligence. I tried this with a group shot of me, TechRadar’s Lance Ulanoff and Apple’s CEO John Ternus and Joz. It added a plant that wasn’t there and extended Lance’s arm. It’s a bit cool but also kinda creepy. Clean Up also gets a performance boost, making it faster to remove unwanted objects or people from your photos.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Design and colors
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/4ALsrPjxc7ma3q24FGt74K.jpg) 
Most people would find it challenging to tell the difference between the iPhone 18 Pro series and iPhone 17 Pro phones. But there’s a couple of telltale signs.
First, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have new colors, and Apple has done a better job of color matching the plateau and back glass of these phones. It’s no longer a two-tone look. I tested the Glacier (blue) version of the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the Burgundy iPhone 18 Pro. I prefer the Glacier, but Burgundy has a sophistication to it. You can also take your pick from Black or Silver.
 ![iPhone 18 Pro Max Dynamic Island](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/YFaQPPunbPf8e2qXHbeL55.jpg) 
The other key visual change is a smaller Dynamic Island. Apple moved the infrared sensor for Face ID under the display, allowing for a tinier cutout at the top of the display. Plus, you can now have up to three Live activities running at once inside the Dynamic Island area, such as a timer, Spotify and Uber status.
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Weight | 
| iPhone 18 Pro | 7.44 oz (211 g) | 
| iPhone 18 Pro Max | 8.78 oz (249 g) | 
| iPhone 17 Pro | 7.27 oz (206 g) | 
| iPhone 17 Pro Max | 8.22 oz (233 g) | 
Perhaps owing to the bigger batteries, variable aperture lens camera and larger vapor chambers, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are heftier than their predecessors despite having the same dimensions as before. At least they fit in the same cases as the 17 Pro series if you're upgrading.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Displays
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/dgQFoMHqkAGoahKiFKYdrd.jpg) 
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max once again offer 6.3-inch and 6.9-inch displays with 120Hz refresh rates and rated 3,000 nits of maximum brightness. These panels are identical versus the iPhone 17 Pro series, but if you’re coming from an iPhone 16 Pro or Pro Max you’ll appreciate the anti-reflective coating.
In our lab tests, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max delivered strong results. Using our Klein K10-A probe combined with the Patterns Mobile iOS app, we measured a maximum brightness of 2,326 nits in a 25% window and 1,762 nits in a 10% window. The iPhone 18 Pro hit a similar 2,314 and 1,627.
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone 17 Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/4edCqgzDe6Geozici7QFqK.jpg) 
The iPhone 17 Pro Max scored 2,324 in a 25% window and 1,882 at 10%, so comparable performance. We have not yet tested the iPhone 17 Pro for comparison.
The Galaxy S26 Ultra doesn’t support the Patterns Mobile app, but we measured HDR brightness in a 10% window with the same equipment. It reached 1,478 nits.
iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone Duo
 ![Apple iPhone Duo shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ENFN2u4hpSYiQYfbA6WbcL.jpg) 
If you’re on the fence between the $1,299 iPhone 18 Pro Max and $1,999 iPhone Duo, here’s a quick cheat sheet. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the phone to get if you want a telephoto camera for better zooming and the longest possible battery life. Plus, only the iPhone 18 Pro Max offers Face ID; the Duo uses Touch ID.
The iPhone Duo is the phone for you if you want the ability to have a small phone and tablet in the same device. You get a larger 7.6-inch main display, versus 6.9 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, plus the ability to run two apps side by side. It’s the better choice for watching videos and multitasking.
Verdict
 ![Apple iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max shown in hand](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ZhVLRJCFGxVjGeDa3TaWmK.jpg) 
My take on the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max is that they are obscenely powerful phones inside a quiet redesign. You get the fastest chip ever in a phone with the A20 Pro, a variable aperture camera I find easy to use and overdue Pro controls that give you more creative freedom when shooting photos and videos.
I personally really like the ability to transform your pics and clips after the fact, whether it’s reframing your shots or adding a Cinematic effect to your footage. And while Siri AI is no Gemini killer, Apple has made great strides with its assistant to the point where it’s a lot more helpful in the moment. I can guarantee you’ll wind up using other chatbots less.
Between the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, I’d opt for the Pro Max because of the bigger screen and longer battery life, but the regular 18 Pro is no slouch and an hour better than the 17 Pro based on our testing.
I think the Galaxy S26 Ultra is still the phone to beat when it comes to zooming power and AI features, but it’s not nearly as fast as the iPhone 18 Pros and lasts two hours less on a charge versus the Max.
Sure, Apple is expected to completely reinvent the iPhone with the iPhone XX/iPhone 20 next year with a rumored all-screen design. But if you want the most powerful iPhone ever in a familiar body, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are easily the best non-folding phones money can buy.
![Mark Spoonauer](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/wtAspSzVfcKLB4JEd39AMo.jpg) 
Mark Spoonauer is the global editor in chief of Tom's Guide and has covered technology for over 20 years. In addition to overseeing the direction of Tom's Guide, Mark specializes in covering all things mobile, having reviewed dozens of smartphones and other gadgets. He has spoken at key industry events and appears regularly on TV to discuss the latest trends, including Cheddar, Fox Business and other outlets. Mark was previously editor in chief of Laptop Mag, and his work has appeared in Wired, Popular Science and Inc. Follow him on Twitter at @mspoonauer.
